title: Magic Quantum Code Surgery
abstract: Non-Clifford operations required for universal quantum computation can be implemented by measuring logical Clifford operators. We present a generalized framework to fault-tolerantly measure transversal Clifford logical operators in quantum low-density parity check (QLDPC) codes. Our protocol takes any QLDPC code and deforms the code across additional ancillary qubits such that a product of stabilizers measures the desired logical Clifford operator. We prove that the deformed, Clifford-stabilized code remains LDPC and that its distance is preserved up to a constant factor independent of the number of physical qubits. We further prove that the Clifford measurement has a fault distance against data qubit and measurement errors that grows linearly with the distance of the original code. We apply our methods to implement logical non-Clifford gates in algorithmically relevant subroutines and to prepare magic states in quantum stabilizer codes.
summary:
**TL;DR** This paper gives a general "gauging" recipe that turns any QLDPC stabilizer code with a transversal logical Clifford symmetry into a deformed, Clifford-stabilized code whose stabilizer group contains the desired logical Clifford operator as a product of checks — so measuring the deformed code's syndrome measures the logical Clifford, yielding magic. The deformed code is proved to remain LDPC with distance degraded only by an $n$-independent constant, and the measurement protocol is shown to have spacetime fault distance $\Theta(d)$ against data and measurement errors. Applications include preparing $k$ unentangled $\ket{+\mathrm{CX}}$ states (hence $\sim 2k/9$ Toffoli states) on any pair of CSS QLDPC blocks, and a controlled-Clifford gadget that parallelizes SWAP networks with $O(\log K)$ Clifford measurements instead of $O(bK)$ $T$ gates.

**The big picture** Universal quantum computing needs non-Clifford resources, usually supplied by magic state distillation, which is expensive. An alternative is to measure a logical Clifford operator directly: the post-measurement state is itself magical. This work provides a general, code-agnostic surgery framework for doing such measurements fault-tolerantly on high-rate low-density codes, together with proofs that the enlarged code stays sparse and protective, and shows how to turn the resulting magic into algorithmically useful primitives rather than exotic entangled states.

**Key contributions**
- A gauging construction on a "gauging 2-complex" (vertices = local factors of the transversal Clifford, edges = gauge qudits, faces = flux checks) valid for any order-$p$ transversal Clifford symmetry on qudits, not just qubit $\mathbb{Z}_2$ cases.
- Proof that the gauged code is LDPC and that its distance is preserved up to a constant independent of $n,k,d$, plus a spacetime fault distance growing linearly in $d$.
- Algorithm producing $\ket{+\mathrm{CX}}^{\otimes k}$ product magic states using only transversal $\mathrm{CX}$ between two blocks of the *same* CSS code — no extra code structure required — with $\Theta(k)$ measurements and expected $4/3$ repetitions per logical pair.
- A $\mathrm{C}\mathsf{T}$ gadget: one Clifford measurement of $X_c \mathsf{T}_t X_a$ plus a $Z_c$ measurement deterministically applies a controlled-Clifford with a shared control across many targets (control teleported to ancilla).

**How it works** Stabilizers that don't commute with $\mathsf{T}$ are symmetrized and then "decorated" with controlled-Pauli and generalized phase gates along rooted paths on the gauging graph; new vertex checks $\mathbb{A}_v = \mathsf{T}_v\prod_{e\in\delta v}X_e$ multiply to $\mathsf{T}$, and cycle checks fix gauge redundancy. Commutation is verified via group-commutator identities (the Clifford condition $[S,\mathsf{T}]$ Pauli is what makes decorations local). Examples include $XS$ gauging on the color code under several vertex-set partitions.

**Why it matters** Supplies a plug-in magic-generation primitive for high-rate QLDPC architectures, where addressable logical non-Clifford gates are scarce; the exponential reduction in non-Clifford cost for QROM SWAP networks and hidden-cut algorithms is concrete algorithmic payoff.

**Caveats** No numerical threshold or decoder simulations are presented; constants (weight blowup, distance factor) are unquantified and could be large. The protocol requires physically implementable non-Clifford entangling gates (controlled-$\mathsf{T}$-type, $CZ$, phase gates) on hardware, and multi-block measurements may need adapter constructions. Magic yield per round ($2k/9$ Toffolis) is modest and relies on a probabilistic $4/9$ conversion.

\begin{abstract}
In Part I, we introduced a general framework for constructing logical gates in quantum CSS codes from cohomology invariants, focusing on \emph{cup products} and their generalizations from topological to qLDPC codes.
In particular, we produced a family of $C^{k-1}Z$ logical gates that we called copy-cup on $k$ copies of the same quantum code implemented by finite-depth circuits.  

Here, we vastly extend this framework by introducing \emph{twists} incorporating code automorphisms, \emph{higher} twisted cohomology operations, and \emph{folding} operations in relative cohomology. The framework includes operations lifting coefficients from $\Z/2$ to $\Z/2^k$, enabling all diagonal logical gates such as single-qubit rotations $\op{R}(2\pi/2^k)$.
Composing these operations with maps that select cohomology classes yields \emph{addressable} logical gates. 
Examples include addressable $T$ gates on three- and four-tori and gates in qLDPC codes beyond topological ones.

We introduce cohomology operations, such as the higher twisted Pontryagin powers, that to our knowledge have not previously appeared in the mathematics literature.
These operations arise from $E_\infty$-structures on cochains, with explicit constructions using cyclic resolutions and the surjection operad.
We expect these results to be of independent interest in homotopy theory. 
Our formalism applies much more broadly to chain complexes carrying suitable operadic structures, and we expect this operadic perspective to uncover further connections between homotopy theory and
fault-tolerant quantum gates.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires the construction of \emph{fault-tolerant logical gates}, which are implemented by a physical circuit that limits the spread of errors.
Logical gates implemented by constant-depth circuits consisting of bounded-size gates are arguably the most efficient way of achieving this. 
Finding a systematic framework for constructing such circuits is the subject of this paper and its first part, Cups and Gates I~\cite{CupsAndGates}.

Early constructions of fault-tolerant logical gates were tied to specific codes, such as the transversal Clifford and $T$ gates in the family of color codes~\cite{Bombin_2007,KubicaYoshidaPastawski15} or families of toric codes in $d$ dimensions~\cite{VasmerBrown3D,4DTCnonClifford}. 
The theorem of Bravyi and K\"onig~\cite{BravyiKoenig2013} bounds the level of the Clifford hierarchy reachable by constant-depth \emph{local} circuits in $D$-dimensional topological codes.
However, it is far less well understood what becomes possible with the long-range connectivity of more general qLDPC codes~\cite{burton2020limitations,FuZhengLiLiu25}. 
With the advent of high-rate qLDPC codes~\cite{BreuckmannEberhardt2021} the question has become pressing, since few of the long-established techniques apply to them directly.\footnote{Other complementary techniques include gate teleportation and magic-state distillation~\cite{GottesmanChuang99,BravyiKitaev05}, code switching~\cite{PaetznickReichardt2013,AndersonDuclosCianciPoulin2014,BombinGaugeCC}, lattice and code surgery~\cite{HorsmanSurgery,CohenSurgery,CowtanSurgery}, pieceable fault tolerance~\cite{YoderPartitioning}, automorphism and fold-transversal gates~\cite{GrasslRoetteler2013,Moussa2016,foldtransversalgates,Quintavalle_2023,EberhardtSteffan2024,SayginelEtAl2024}, and computer search~\cite{WebsterSearch}.}

\paragraph{Cohomology invariants are logical gates.}
In Part I~\cite{CupsAndGates}, we built a framework to construct fault-tolerant logical gates based on \emph{cohomology invariants}, which we recall now.
In a CSS code, physical computational basis states $\ket{a}$ are labeled by cochains $a\in A^q$, while logical states $\ket{[a]}$ arise from the superposition of all representatives of a cohomology class $[a]\in H^q(A)$. A cohomology invariant is a function $\Phi\colon A^q\to\Z/2^s$ whose value on a cocycle depends only on its cohomology class. 
Hence, the diagonal unitary
\[
 U_\Phi\ket a=\exp\bigl(2\pi i\,\Phi(a)/2^s\bigr)\ket a
\]
preserves the code space and acts on the logical basis state $\ket{[a]}$ by applying the corresponding phase. 
The unitary $U_\Phi$ is realized by a circuit that is the product of (multi-controlled) phase rotations. 
The cohomology operations $\Phi$ that we describe here are all \emph{local} themselves in the sense that they are a sum of terms each of which depends on a bounded number of bits, with every bit occurring in a bounded number of terms. 
This in turn implies that they yield a constant-depth physical circuit. 
Cohomology thus connects a global feature, the logical action, to a local one, the circuit, and all computations of logical actions can be carried out at the level of cohomology. 
The resulting circuits are often quite unintuitive, and it is unlikely that many of them could have been found by hand or by brute-force search.

Common sources of cohomology invariants are \emph{cohomology operations} such as the \emph{cup product}, together with an integral. For degree-one cocycles $x_1,\ldots,x_r$ with $\F_2$ coefficients on a closed triangulated $r$-manifold $X$, the integral
\[
 \int_X x_1\cup x_2\cup\cdots\cup x_r
\]
is a cohomology invariant that counts the parity of the multilinear (degree-$r$) intersection of the dual cycles $\{x_i^*\}$.
In topological codes, this immediately gives finite-depth logical gates, such as the $CZ$ gate between two copies of the two-dimensional toric code and the $CCZ$ gate between three copies of the three-dimensional toric code~\cite{Yoshida15,Yoshida16,Yoshida17,KubicaYoshidaPastawski15,Barkeshli23,Barkeshli24_2,Chen2023higher,Wang2023,Zhu2023}.

In Part I~\cite{CupsAndGates} of this work, and related concurrent papers \cite{lin2024transversal,golowich2024quantum}, the notion of cup product was generalized to qLDPC codes. To achieve this, we first defined cup products for classical codes which we then showed to induce cup products on their tensor and balanced products. We identified a structure weaker than a differential graded algebra that is sufficient for the new operation to be a cohomology invariant.\footnote{The condition for invariance that we found was that the product need not be associative, and the Leibniz rule only needs to hold after integration. This condition can be checked locally on the parity-check matrices, in a way reminiscent of triorthogonality~\cite{BravyiHaah2012}, and does not require an underlying manifold.}
As a result, we constructed the \emph{copy-cup} gates: 
given $r$ copies of a qLDPC quantum code equipped with an $r$-fold cup product, the phase $(-1)^{\int x_1\cup\cdots\cup x_r}$ is implemented by a constant-depth circuit of physical $C^{r-1}Z$ gates between the blocks. When the invariant is nontrivial, it implements a logical gate consisting of the $C^{r-1}Z$ acting on various combinations of logical qubits, which is at the $r$-th level of Clifford hierarchy, up to lower-level corrections. 

On the constructive side, cup products beyond manifolds were used to find qLDPC codes with constant-depth non-Clifford gates in finite-length tricycle codes and balanced product codes~\cite{MenonMagicTricycles2026,JacobMcLauchlanBrowne2025,LiPreskillXu25,TiewBreuckmann2026}, as well as in families of almost-good and good qLDPC codes which are also locally testable~\cite{LiLiLiu26almostgood,LiLiLiu26good}, and codes with constant-weight stabilizers whose transversal $C^{r-1}Z$ gates surpass the previously known trade-off between length, distance and number of logical gates~\cite{GolowichTamoZhu2026}.
On the conceptual side, Poincar\'e duality and cup and cap products have been established for sheaf codes~\cite{LiLiLiuNguyen25}, together with a general theory of cohomological invariants of hypergraph-product and sheaf codes~\cite{LiShaoWeiLiLiu26}, and no-go theorems constrain which gates product codes can support~\cite{FuZhengLiLiu25}. 

\paragraph{What was missing, and the new ideas.}
Despite this progress, some of the most basic desiderata remained out of reach. 
We want non-Clifford gates \emph{within a single code block}, and ideally, we also want to \emph{address} individual logical qubits. 
The desired framework needs to capture rotation gates, such as $T=\op{diag}(1,e^{2\pi i/8})$. 
Since the phase associated to an integral of products of $\Z/2$-cocycles is a sign, ordinary cup products are not sufficient for producing the eighth roots of unity that $T$ requires. 
Finally, we want constructions which apply beyond topological codes. 
This paper addresses all of these points by introducing novel cohomology invariants, which we describe now.

One of the ways to obtain new operations is to incorporate symmetries of the cochain complex\footnote{For example, in the case of topological codes, the symmetries can be simply spatial symmetries. More generally, these are automorphisms of the cochain complex of the code.} into cohomology operations.
Additionally, we can \emph{lift coefficients}, say from $\Z/2$ to~$\Z/8$, which forces correction terms that use the higher homotopies expressing the fact that the cup product is only commutative up to homotopy.
These homotopies can be organized in an $E_\infty$-structure and the language of operads which allows us to systematically construct \emph{higher twisted cohomology operations} generalizing (higher) Pontryagin squares.

We introduce further ideas in order to make the resulting gates addressable. 
One of them is that we select the logical inputs by composing the cohomology operation with cochain maps that act non-trivially on different cohomology classes including removing some of them from the expression while retaining cohomology invariance.

Lastly, another idea is to use symmetries of the cochain complex to ``fold'' it in a nontrivial way and consider relative cohomology operations on the ``folded'' complex. 

Together, these ideas produce many addressable classes of new operations. In particular, we obtain individually addressable $T$ gates on toric codes in three and four dimensions, as well as addressable non-Clifford gates on further manifolds, and on qLDPC codes which are not associated with manifolds.
To our knowledge, many of the operations here have not been studied in the mathematics literature before, and we expect them to be of independent interest in homotopy theory. 

\subsection{Main contributions}
\label{sec:main-contributions}

We now explain the ideas of the paper in more detail, in the order in which they build on each other.

\paragraph{Twisting by a symmetry.}
Assume that the cochain complex has automorphism group~$G$, so the action of elements $g\in G$ descends to cohomology. Then, the \emph{twisted cup product}
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-twisted-power}
 \int_X x\cup g_2x\cup\cdots\cup g_rx,
 \qquad g_i\in G,
\end{equation}
is a cohomology invariant of the single class $x$. Intuitively, this yields non-trivial outcomes for classes $x$ that intersect with elements in their $G$-orbit.
Nothing in this argument requires $g$ to be invertible. In fact, any endomorphism $F$ of the code complex can be substituted into a multilinear invariant, $\int F_1(x)\cup\cdots\cup F_r(x)$, and the result is again a cohomology invariant. 
This gives single-block gates of $CCZ$ type on the three-torus, on products of a surface with a circle, and on the tricycle and Golowich--Tamo--Zhu codes discussed in \Cref{sec:non-clifford-fold-transversal-gates}.

\paragraph{Lifting coefficients and $E_\infty$-structure.}
Twisted cup products over $\Z/2$ can only produce gates of $C^{r-1}Z$ type. For other phase gates, such as the $T$ gate, we need invariants valued in $\Z/2^k$. The naive attempt is to read the bits of a cocycle $x\in Z^q(X;\Z/2)$ as the integers $0$ and $1$, which defines a non-linear inclusion map $\iota$ with values in $C^q(X;\Z)$. Denoting $\widetilde x= \iota x$, we can form $\int\widetilde x\cup g_2\widetilde x\cup\cdots$, say, modulo $8$. The problem is that $\widetilde x$ need not be a cocycle. Its coboundary vanishes modulo $2$, but need not vanish over $\Z$. As a consequence, such a naive expression is not a cohomology operation.

The \emph{Pontryagin square} is the simplest example of repairing this in the untwisted case with only two inputs. The expression
\[
 \Po^{(2)}(x)=\widetilde x\cup\widetilde x+\widetilde x\cup_1 d\widetilde x
 \pmod 4
\]
is a well-defined operation $H^q(X;\Z/2)\to H^{2q}(X;\Z/4)$ for even $q$. 
The \emph{correction term} $\widetilde x\cup_1d\widetilde x$ involves Steenrod's cup-$1$ product $\cup_1 $ and vanishes when $\widetilde x$ is already closed modulo four. 
It makes the expression a cocycle whose cohomology class is independent of the chosen lift and cocycle representative (\Cref{sec:integral-lifts}).
The Pontryagin square is the prototype of the general form of cohomology operations in this paper, whose leading term is typically an $r$-fold cup power, plus correction terms built from coboundaries and higher cup products, such that the sum is a cohomology invariant with finer coefficients.

The cup-$1$ product supplies the homotopy between the cup product and its graded opposite. The cancellation modulo four uses both its cochain identity and the divisibility of $d\widetilde x$ by two. The same mechanism in higher arity requires homotopies between the $r$-fold cup product and its permutations, homotopies between these homotopies, and so on. Such coherent systems of higher homotopies form an \emph{$E_\infty$-structure} on cochains~\cite[Section~3]{May1972}. To make these operations explicit, we use the surjection operad $\cX$, constructed by McClure--Smith and Berger--Fresse~\cite{McClureSmith2003,BergerFresse2004}. Its elements are words whose action is defined by cutting simplices into overlapping faces. The word $(1,2)$ gives the cup product, $(1,2,1)$ gives its commutativity homotopy, and $(1,2,\ldots,r)$ gives the $r$-fold cup product. The word $(1,2,3,4,1)$ gives a homotopy between the fourfold cup product and its cyclic permutation. The differential of the operad records the identities relating these operations.

Since we want to twist by symmetries, say by a subgroup $G$ of the symmetric group $\Sigma_r$, it is particularly useful to organize the corresponding homotopies using a free resolution~$W$ of~$\Z$ over~$\Z[G]$. 
A $G$-equivariant chain map $W\to\cX(r)$~\cite{KMM2021} turns each generator~$e_{i,j}$ into an $r$-input cochain operation~$\mu^G_{i,j}$ lowering the total degree by~$i$. 
Here $\mu^G_{0,0}$ is the $r$-fold cup product, the $\mu^G_{1,j}$ give homotopies between its permutations, and the $\mu^G_{2,j}$ give homotopies between these homotopies. Their identities are encoded by the differential of~$W$.
For the simple case $G=C_2$ this recovers Steenrod's higher cup products. We explain the construction in \Cref{sec:cohomology-operations}.

\paragraph{Twisting and lifting at the same time.}
These operations can be combined to obtain \emph{twisted higher cohomology operations} which are the mathematical heart of this paper. 

Let $G$ be a finite abelian group acting on the cochain complex $C^*(X;\Z/\theta)$ and permuting the $r=|G|$ inputs of a cochain operation. Let $\omega\colon G\to\{\pm1\}$ record whether $g$ preserves or reverses the orientation, and let $M=M(\theta)[-q]$ be Steenrod's universal complex, which is freely generated by $u$ and $v$ with $du=\theta v$. A cocycle $x$ with $\Z/\theta$ coefficients together with its lift to a ring $R$, say  $\widetilde x$, can be packaged as a chain map $f_x\colon M\to C^*(X;R)$ with $f_x(u)=\widetilde x$ and $f_x(v)=\beta_\theta(x)=(d\widetilde x)/\theta$. The whole construction is contained in the following diagram of chain maps:
\begin{equation*}\label{eq:intro-evaluation-diagram}
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3.4em]
 \operatorname{ev}_x: W\otimes_{\Z[G]}\bigl(R_\omega\otimes M^{\otimes r}\bigr)
   \arrow[r,"\mathrm{id}\otimes f_x^{\otimes r}"]
 & W\otimes_{\Z[G]}\bigl(R_\omega\otimes C^*(X;R)^{\otimes r}\bigr)
   \arrow[r,"E"]
 & R.
\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation*}
The object on the left is \emph{universal}: it depends only on the group $G$, the resolution $W$, the coefficients $\theta$ and $R$, the degree $q$ and the character $\omega$, but \emph{not} on the specific cochain complex. 
Only finitely many terms contribute in each total degree, so its homology, the universal twisted homology $H_n(G;R_\omega\otimes M^{\otimes r})$, can be computed by finite linear algebra.
A cycle representative $z=\sum e_{i,j}\otimes m_{i,j}$ of a homology class can be thought of as a recipe for constructing a cohomology invariant: 
$m_{i,j}$ is a linear combination of tensor words in $u$ and $v$, and $e_{i,j}$ says which generalized cup-$i$ product to apply to it.

The first map in the diagram, $\mathrm{id}\otimes f_x^{\otimes r}$, substitutes $\widetilde x$ and $\beta_\theta(x)$ for $u$ and $v$, and the second map $E$ applies the operation $\mu^G_{i,j}$ to the inputs \emph{translated along the $G$-orbit}, $(a_1,\dots,a_r)\mapsto(g_1a_1,\dots,g_ra_r)$, and integrates over $X$.  
Since all maps are chain maps, a cycle $z$ on the left defines a cohomology invariant
\[
 \Phi_{[z]}\colon H^q(X;\Z/\theta)\longrightarrow R,
 \qquad [x]\longmapsto\operatorname{ev}_x(z).
\]
To obtain a physical circuit, we choose a representative satisfying a divisibility condition that makes its formula defined on arbitrary cochains, as explained in \Cref{sec:lifts-to-cochain-operations}.

For $G=C_2$ acting trivially on $X$, $\theta=2$ and $R=\Z/4$, the cycle $z=e_0\otimes u\otimes u+2e_1\otimes u\otimes v$ recovers the (integrated) Pontryagin square.

For $G=C_4$, we construct an operation lifting coefficients from $\Z/2$ to $\Z/8$, and for $G=C_3$ one lifting coefficients from $\Z/3$ to $\Z/9$. Combined with the cochain maps described below, these give individually addressable qubit $T$ gates on the four-dimensional toric code and qutrit $T$ gates on the three-dimensional toric code, respectively (\Cref{sec:the-four-torus,sec:qutrits-and-the-three-torus}).

\paragraph{Addressability by cochain maps.}
The logical gates arising from these twisted operations typically act on all logical qubits at once. To isolate an operation on a single cohomology class, we use the following simple observation. 
If $\Phi$ is a cohomology invariant on a complex $D$ and $F\colon C\to D$ is a cochain map, then $\Phi\circ F$ is a cohomology invariant on $C$, with logical action $[a]\mapsto\Phi([Fa])$. 
The map $F$ is substituted into the phase, not implemented as a unitary, so it need neither be invertible nor commute with the symmetry defining $\Phi$. 
Whenever $F$ removes support on a cohomology class, the gate acts as the identity on the corresponding logical qubits, which gives addressability.

Concrete bounded-weight maps come from \emph{circle folds}. Folding a circle onto a semicircle, $s\colon S^1\to S^1$, satisfies $s^2=s$, so $s^*$ and $1-s^*$ are complementary cochain projections. On cohomology, $s^*$ retains $H^0$ and kills $H^1$, while $1-s^*$ does the reverse. On products of circles, these maps can be combined with coordinate permutations and sums to select individual logical directions or parities (\Cref{sec:circle-fold-projections}).

To summarize, the toolbox for addressing gates includes:
\begin{itemize}
 \item \emph{Pullbacks} along cellular maps, and cochain maps between code complexes in general, transport a cohomology invariant from one complex to another: $\Phi\mapsto\Phi\circ F$.
 \item \emph{Folds and cochain projections}, such as the circle fold $s^*$ and its complement $1-s^*$, select part of the logical information, making a gate act on chosen logical qubits or parities.
 \item \emph{Relative cochains} $C^*(X,Y)$, vanishing on a subcomplex $Y$, incorporate boundary conditions, generalizing the smooth and rough boundaries of surface codes. Folds naturally produce relative cochains, for example, $1-s^*$ vanishes on the fixed semicircle.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Relative cohomology and folds.}
Symmetries enter in another way through folding and relative cohomology. The starting point is a logical $T$ gate on three copies of a surface code on a tetrahedron with coupled boundary conditions~\cite{HsinKobayashiZhu2024,Bauer_2025,Davydova_2026}. Its $\Z/8$-valued phase combines a triple cup product in the bulk with correction terms on a face and an edge.

Our observation is that all three inputs can be supplied by a single surface code on a cube with relative boundary conditions on two opposite faces. Coordinate permutations fold three tetrahedral regions onto one tetrahedron, and suitable combinations of the folded cochains satisfy the required boundary conditions. This gives a constant-depth $T$ gate on the single logical qubit of the three-dimensional surface code (\Cref{sec:relative-t-cube}). Circle folds and pullbacks then transport this operation to individually addressable $T$ gates on the three-dimensional toric code (\Cref{sec:relative-t-three-torus}).

The construction extends to suitable manifold codes and, through bounded-weight cochain maps, to our tricycle and three-dimensional tile-code examples (\Cref{sec:relative-t-further-examples,sec:relative-t-beyond-manifolds,sec:addressable-tt-example}). Higher-dimensional versions give higher rotation gates whenever the corresponding simplex operation is available.

In our examples we did nothing to optimize the depth of the circuits, and there is a lot of room to do so. First, every operation lives in an equivalence class: cohomologous universal cocycles $z$, different resolutions $W$, and different comparison maps $W\to\cX(r)$ all give the same logical gate but have different cochain-level expressions. Searching within an equivalence class for a representative of small depth is a concrete optimization problem. Second, coefficients may be lifted before or after applying the cochain maps which make a gate addressable, and these maps are themselves far from unique. Third, the symmetry~$G$, the automorphisms, and the folds can all be chosen differently, and for a given target gate set some choices will lead to much shallower circuits than others. We leave such optimizations to future work.

\subsection{Comparison with the literature}
\label{sec:comparison-with-literature}

\paragraph{Topological codes and the symmetries picture.}
For topological codes, constant-depth logical gates have long been understood through symmetry-protected topological phases and the cohomology operations describing their responses, in particular cup products and their higher versions~\cite{Yoshida15,Yoshida16,Yoshida17,Barkeshli23,Barkeshli24_1,Barkeshli24_2,Chen2023higher,Chen23,Wang2023,Zhu2023,HsinKobayashiZhu2024}. The twisted operations of this paper differ in that a symmetry of the space enters the operation itself; a few examples of this have been known as gates on folded triangles and on tetrahedra~\cite{HsinKobayashiZhu2024}, but this paper goes far beyond that.

\paragraph{Fold-transversal gates.}
Fold-transversal Clifford gates~\cite{Moussa2016,foldtransversalgates,Quintavalle_2023,EberhardtSteffan2024,SayginelEtAl2024} use an automorphism of the code together with the intersection form, and more generally, code automorphisms give Clifford gates~\cite{GrasslRoetteler2013}. Our results show the non-Clifford extensions that are somewhat similar in spirit: automorphisms are substituted into a multilinear cohomology invariant; they also enter inside the homotopies of the $E_\infty$-structure, which is what allows the coefficients to be lifted.

\paragraph{Constructions of qLDPC codes with non-Clifford gates.}
Cup products on sheaf codes and products of algebraic codes~\cite{lin2024transversal,golowich2024quantum}, on homological product codes~\cite{Zhu25topological,Zhu25systolic}, on tricycle and related product codes~\cite{MenonMagicTricycles2026,JacobMcLauchlanBrowne2025,TiewBreuckmann2026,LiPreskillXu25}, on almost-good and good locally testable codes~\cite{LiLiLiu26almostgood,LiLiLiu26good} and on the codes of Golowich, Tamo and Zhu~\cite{GolowichTamoZhu2026} all produce multi-block $C^{r-1}Z$ gates of copy-cup type. 

Our new contribution shows how to fold such gates into a single block and also how to make them addressable. 

\paragraph{Homological frameworks for logical gates.}
Several recent works develop general homological descriptions of logical gates on qLDPC codes. Li, Li, Liu and Nguyen~\cite{LiLiLiuNguyen25} establish Poincar\'e duality and cup and cap products for sheaf codes. Li, Shao, Wei, Li and Liu~\cite{LiShaoWeiLiLiu26} develop a theory of (co)homological invariants of hypergraph-product and sheaf codes. These multiplicative structures provide starting points for our universal construction, provided they extend to generalized cup-$i$ products with a compatible symmetry and integral.

Sahay, Long and Khemani~\cite{SahayLongKhemani26} develop a concurrent framework for logical gates and addressability based on general chain maps between code complexes, without restricting to maps arising from cup products and their higher homotopies. It organizes diagonal gates of $C^{\ell-1}Z$ type between $\ell$ code blocks by the homology of the tensor product of the $\ell$ code complexes; in the language of \Cref{sec:logical-gates-from-invariants} these are exactly the $\Z/2$-multilinear cohomology invariants, and the classification is an instance of the K\"unneth theorem. 
Every such logical action is realized by some cycle, in general a dense one.
Gates are found by sparsifying it with boundaries, when possible, and reading off the circuit. 
A multi-block pattern applied within one block yields the symmetrized action. Their examples are the full Clifford group on the two-dimensional toric code, addressable $CCZ$ gates between and within blocks of the three-dimensional toric code, and addressable Clifford and $CCZ$ gates on fracton codes. They obtain diagonal Clifford gates such as $S$ from symmetric chain maps on a suitable lift of the whole code complex to $\Z/4$ coefficients, giving explicit quadratic, non-multilinear phase functions, and point to quadratic homological maps. A full treatment of intra-block non-Clifford gates is left to future work.

Our results and discussion are complementary. Their multilinear diagonal construction produces products of $C^kZ$ gates (including intra-block ones), and they also construct $S$ gates using $\Z/4$-valued quadratic phase functions. 
Our construction here focuses on intra-code gates and supplies explicit coefficient-lifting operations for single-block $T$, $CS$ and higher phase gates.
The universal lifts use the higher homotopies of the $E_\infty$-structure, organized by a resolution of the symmetry group, to construct the correction terms needed for these lifted expressions to descend to cohomology, while the relative construction also uses boundary terms. Sparsity follows automatically from bounded incidence and bounded-weight cochain maps.
Their framework also treats non-diagonal gates and measurement gadgets. We expect the two approaches to combine well to yield much stronger results in the future.

\paragraph{Mathematics.}
Steenrod constructed the cup-$i$ products~\cite{Steenrod1947} and the cyclic reduced powers~\cite{Steenrod1953} and gave the universal description of the Pontryagin square~\cite{Steenrod1957}, Thomas the higher Pontryagin powers~\cite{Thomas1957}, and May gave a general algebraic framework for Steenrod operations~\cite{May1970}. The surjection operad is due to McClure and Smith~\cite{McClureSmith2003} and Berger and Fresse~\cite{BergerFresse2004}, and Kaufmann and Medina-Mardones~\cite{KMM2021} gave the explicit cochain-level formulas for Steenrod operations which we build on. The twisted operations constructed here, which evaluate the higher homotopies along the orbit of a group acting on the space, appear to be novel.

\subsection{Outlook}
\label{sec:outlook}

The universal construction of \Cref{sec:constructing-twisted-cohomology-operations} uses only three things about the space $X$: an action of $G$ on its cochains, an $E_\infty$-type family of generalized cup-$i$ products, and an integral compatible with $G$. Nothing requires $X$ to be a manifold, and the most important open direction is to systematically study these operations on qLDPC codes beyond manifolds. Tensor and balanced products of classical codes with cup products~\cite{CupsAndGates} and the multiplicative structures of~\cite{LiLiLiuNguyen25,LiShaoWeiLiLiu26} are natural candidates for constructing concrete operations.

Another question on the coding theory side is how far addressability reaches. Which gates at a given level of the Clifford hierarchy can be individually addressed, and which logical bases can be reached by these methods? For codes associated with $d$-dimensional spaces, what constraints does the geometry impose on constant-depth circuits with nonlocal connectivity? Such constraints would provide a nonlocal analogue of the Bravyi--K\"onig bound. Finally, we have only begun to exploit $E_\infty$-structures and operads for fault-tolerant quantum computation; we expect this operadic perspective to uncover further connections between homotopy theory and logical gates.

The cup product is a relatively common tool in condensed-matter and high-energy physics. It is used to write down topological actions and exactly solvable lattice models, such as Dijkgraaf--Witten gauge theories~\cite{DijkgraafWitten}, and to describe symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phases~\cite{Chen13} and anomalies of ordinary and higher-form symmetries~\cite{KapustinThorngren14anomalies,kapustin2015higher,Gaiottoetal2015,Barkeshli24_1}. Steenrod's higher cup products~\cite{Steenrod1947} similarly enter lattice descriptions of fermionic phases and bosonization~\cite{GaiottoKapustin16,ChenKapustinRadicevic18,Chen2023higher}.
Cup and higher-cup products have also recently been used to construct
finite-depth non-Clifford logical gates in topological and qLDPC
codes~\cite{HsinKobayashiZhu25,KobayashiZhuHsin26,SahayLongKhemani26},
while closely related group-cohomological constructions and protocols
using non-Abelian topological codes yield phase gates throughout the
Clifford hierarchy and beyond~\cite{HuangWarmanSchaferNamekiChen25,
WarmanSchaferNameki26}; the new invariants developed here may provide
further logical gates in these settings.
More generally, it would be interesting to understand the role of newly found invariants in physics.

On the mathematical side, the universal twisted homology groups $H_n(G;R_\omega\otimes M^{\otimes r})$ and their liftable parts are computable by finite linear algebra, and we have only evaluated them in the cases needed for our examples. Computing them for all finite abelian groups, degrees and coefficients would give a complete classification of twisted cohomology operations of this type, and we expect that each class can be found constructively. The operations themselves seem interesting in homotopy theory in their own right, as cohomology operations for spaces with a group action, and we expect them to admit an interpretation as topological (albeit geometrically non-local) responses of systems with a spatial symmetry.

\subsection{Structure of the paper}
\label{sec:structure}

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows. \Cref{sec:cochain-complexes} contains preliminary material such as cochain complexes, their relation to CSS codes, gates from cohomology operations, as well as some mathematical preliminaries needed later. \Cref{sec:cohomology-operations} introduces the cup-$i$ products and Steenrod squares, the surjection operad and the $E_\infty$-structure on cochains, and derives the generalized cup-$i$ products and the lifting of coefficients.
\Cref{sec:constructing-twisted-cohomology-operations} contains the main mathematical construction: universal twisted elements and their evaluation on a space with symmetry.
\Cref{sec:selecting-cohomology-operations} explains addressability by composing with cochain maps.

The remaining sections are devoted to examples: \Cref{sec:non-clifford-fold-transversal-gates} twists ordinary cup products into single-block gates and shows some addressable examples of them; \Cref{sec:non-clifford-gates-via-twisted-cohomology-operations} shows several applications of lifted-coefficient higher twisted Pontryagin powers; and \Cref{sec:addressable-relative-cup-gates} discusses the relative cohomology operations building on the example of a phase gate on a 3-dimensional tetrahedron that gives a $T$ gate on a cube and a torus; this is further generalized to higher dimensions and to some non-manifold examples.

\section{Addressable Gates using Relative Cohomology}
\label{sec:addressable-relative-cup-gates}

The primary example in this section constructs an addressable $T$ gate on a 3-torus by folding, which requires extending our formalism to operations in relative cohomology. To build up to this example, we first review how the $T$ gate on three glued copies of the toric code on a tetrahedron is obtained from a relative cohomology operation. This is an operation known in the literature~\cite{HsinKobayashiZhu2024,Bauer_2025,Davydova_2026} which was originally understood through the transversal $T$-gate on a color code tetrahedron~\cite{Bombin_2007}. We then show how to use coordinate reflections and relative cochains to obtain a $T$-gate on a cube, which is, to the best of our knowledge, a new operation. This can be extended to an addressable $T$ on a 3-torus by using the circle folds of \Cref{sec:circle-fold-projections}.

\Cref{sec:relative-t-further-examples} extends these ideas to higher dimensions and other manifolds, while \Cref{sec:relative-t-beyond-manifolds} gives examples beyond manifolds.

\subsection{A \texorpdfstring{$T$}{T} gate for three copies of the toric code on a tetrahedron}
\label{sec:relative-t-tetrahedron}

Let ${\mathcal D}=[p_0p_1p_2p_3]$ be an ordered, subdivided tetrahedron, let $\mathcal F_i$ be the face opposite $p_i$, and put ${\mathcal F}={\mathcal F}_0$, $\mathcal E=[p_1p_2]$, and $\eta=[p_0p_1]$. These denote oriented fundamental chains of the subdivided faces and edges, with $\partial {\mathcal D}={\mathcal F}_0-{\mathcal F}_1+{\mathcal F}_2-{\mathcal F}_3$. Consider three copies of the toric code described by a cochain complex on the tetrahedron. For cochains $b=(b_1,b_2,b_3)$, we impose the boundary conditions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tetrahedral-relative-conditions}
 b_i|_{{\mathcal F}_i}=0\quad(i=1,2,3),\qquad (b_1+b_2+b_3)|_{\mathcal F}=0.
\end{equation}
In every degree, these conditions define a subcomplex $\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})\subset C^*({\mathcal D};\Z/2)^3$. 

With these boundary conditions, the relative complex $\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})$ has one-dimensional first cohomology (as we show below), detected by $\lambda(b)=\int_\eta b_1$ for $b\in\mathcal A^1({\mathcal D})$.

Write $\widetilde b_i=\iota(b_i)$ for the coefficientwise $0/1$-lift. We introduce the following cochain operation:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tetrahedral-t-phase}
 \Phi_{\mathcal D}(b)=4\int_{\mathcal D}\widetilde b_1\cup\widetilde b_3\cup\widetilde b_2+2\int_{\mathcal F}\widetilde b_1\cup\widetilde b_2-\int_{\mathcal E}\widetilde b_1\pmod8.
\end{equation}
Expressed as a physical circuit, the three terms above give products of physical $CCZ$, $CS^{\pm1}$, and $T^{\pm1}$ gates on tetrahedra, triangles, and edges, respectively.

The operation $\Phi_{\mathcal D}(b)$ is a cohomology operation:

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:tetrahedral-relative-t}
    Consider the relative cochain complex $\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})$ as discussed above. Then:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The map $\lambda$ identifies $H^1(\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})) \cong \Z/2$, and thus, there is one logical qubit.
        \item The operation $\Phi_{\mathcal D}(b)$ is a cohomology operation corresponding to the logical $T$-gate implemented by $U_{\Phi_{\mathcal D}}$ on this logical qubit. Namely, on cocycles we have
        \begin{equation}\label{eq:tetrahedral-t-action}
        \Phi_{\mathcal D}(b)=\iota(\lambda(b))\in\Z/8.
        \end{equation}
    \end{enumerate}
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $b_i=du_i$ with $u_i(p_0)=0$. Then $u_i|_{\mathcal F_i}=0$, and $u_1+u_2+u_3$ is constant on $\mathcal F$, with value $u_1(p_1)=\lambda(b)$. Thus $b$ is a coboundary in $\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})$ precisely when this constant is zero. Both constants occur, by assigning the value one at each vertex of $\mathcal F$ to a component $u_i$ whose face $\mathcal F_i$ does not contain that vertex, and extending by zero elsewhere.

For a binary one-cocycle $b=du$, the canonical integer lifts satisfy $d\widetilde b=2\widetilde b\cup\widetilde b$ and $d\widetilde u=\widetilde b-2\widetilde u\cup\widetilde b$. The Leibniz rule therefore gives the following identities modulo eight
\begin{align*}
 d(4\widetilde u_1\cup\widetilde b_3\cup\widetilde b_2)&=4\widetilde b_1\cup\widetilde b_3\cup\widetilde b_2 &&\text{on }{\mathcal D}       ,\\
 d(2\widetilde u_1\cup\widetilde b_2)&=4\widetilde u_1\cup\widetilde b_3\cup\widetilde b_2+2\widetilde b_1\cup\widetilde b_2 &&\text{on }{\mathcal F},\\
 -d\widetilde u_1&=2\widetilde u_1\cup\widetilde b_2-\widetilde b_1 &&\text{on }{\mathcal E}.
\end{align*}
Here $b_3=b_1+b_2$ on ${\mathcal F}$ and $b_2=b_1$ on ${\mathcal E}$. Stokes' formula moves the three terms successively from ${\mathcal D}$ to ${\mathcal F}$ to ${\mathcal E}$ and all other faces vanish by~\Cref{eq:tetrahedral-relative-conditions}. The result is $\widetilde u_1(p_1)-\widetilde u_1(p_2)=\iota(\lambda(b))$, since $p_2\in {\mathcal F}_1$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{A \texorpdfstring{$T$}{T} gate on a cube}
\label{sec:relative-t-cube}

In this section, we extend the $T$ gate on the tetrahedron to the cube, and subsequently, we also extend this to a 3-torus. Before proceeding, let us outline the core of the main idea behind this construction. 
We start with a 3-torus $T_L^3$ with the usual cubic cellulation and even $L$. Let $Q=[0,L]^3$, subdivided into unit cubes. Consider the following chain of maps:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-t-roadmap}
 C^1(T^3_L; \Z/2)
 \xrightarrow{\ F_x\ }
 C^1(Q,\partial_xQ; \Z/2)
 \xrightarrow{\ c\,\mapsto\,b(c)\ }
 \mathcal A^1({\mathcal D}; \Z/2)
 \xrightarrow{\ \Phi_{\mathcal D}\ }
 \Z/8,
\end{equation}
which contains the following steps.
\begin{enumerate}
 \item \emph{Selecting one direction on the torus.} More specifically, the map $F_x$ is a composition of two maps, which together take us from a torus to a cube with boundary conditions giving one-dimensional first cohomology,
 \begin{equation} \label{eq:pair-maps}
 C^1(T^3_L; \Z/2)
 \xrightarrow{\ 1+s_x^*\ }
 C^1(T^3_L,A_x; \Z/2)
 \xrightarrow{\ p^*\ }
 C^1(Q,\partial_xQ; \Z/2)
\end{equation}
A circle fold $s_x$ (introduced in \Cref{sec:circle-fold-projections})
 turns a cochain $a$ on the 3-torus into the cochain $a+s_x^*a$, which
 vanishes on the fixed set $A_x = I_+ \times T_L^2$. Pulling back along the
 quotient map $p\colon Q\to T^3_L$ gives a cochain on the cube
 which vanishes on the two faces $x=0$ and $x=L$.  On cohomology this step
 retains exactly the logical qubit belonging to the $x$-direction. The total cochain map $F_x = p^* (1+s_x^*)$ is the map we use for the precomposition in order to make a gate on a cube addressable.
 \item \emph{$T$ gate on the cube}. The cube is the union of six tetrahedra, which are
 permuted by the coordinate permutations.  One only needs to consider half of them. Intuitively, it is because half of the cube is topologically still a cube, so restricting to half a cube does not lose any homological information. Then, one can fold three tetrahedra belonging to a half of the cube into a single one. The action of the coordinate permutation can be then used to show that there exists a basis for the one-cocycles in which the boundary conditions coincide with the tetrahedral boundary conditions we have seen earlier. Finally, we can apply the relative cohomology operation $\Phi_{\mathcal D}$.
\end{enumerate}

Subdivide each unit cube into its six coordinate-order tetrahedra and order vertices lexicographically by $(x+y+z,x,y,z)$. The coordinate permutations
\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}

\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}
oriented in this order. In particular, $\mathcal F=\{z=L\}\cap {\mathcal D}$, $\mathcal F_1=\{y=z\}\cap {\mathcal D}$, $\mathcal F_2=\{x=y\}\cap {\mathcal D}$, and $\mathcal F_3=\{x=0\}\cap {\mathcal D}$.

Consider the three tetrahedra $\mathcal D$, $r_{12}\mathcal D$ and $\rho \mathcal D$ that form half of the cube: $\{(x,y,z) \in Q:  \ y \leq z\}$. For a cochain $c \in C^1(Q, \partial_x Q; \Z/2)$, folding $r_{12}\mathcal D$ and $\rho \mathcal D$ onto $\mathcal D$ gives the pullbacks $r_{12}^*c$ and $\rho^*c$, respectively. \begin{equation}\label{eq:cube-reflection-inputs}

\end{equation}
The first two of them vanish on the mirror planes $\mathcal F_1$ and $\mathcal F_2$, and the third vanishes on $\mathcal F_3\subset {\partial_x Q}$. Their sum is $\rho^*c$, which vanishes on $\mathcal F$ because $\rho(\mathcal F)\subset\{x=L\}$. Namely, for the new cochain $b = (b_1,b_2,b_3)$ defined above, the tetrahedral boundary conditions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cube-tetrahedral-conditions}

\end{equation}
are satisfied.
Thus~\Cref{eq:cube-reflection-inputs} is a cochain map into $\mathcal A^*({\mathcal D})$ that maps $c \mapsto b(c)$. These are pullbacks of absolute cochains followed by restriction: the individual reflections need not preserve ${\partial_x Q}$. In particular, these cochains do not need to be extended to the entire cube because they already satisfy the correct boundary conditions and vanish where appropriate.

\begin{equation}

\end{equation}
We provide the full expression for completeness, with binary sums taken
before the coefficientwise $0/1$-lift:
\begin{align}

  \iota(r_{12}^*c+\rho^*c)\cup\widetilde c\cup\iota(c+r_{12}^*c)\notag\\

\end{align}

\begin{equation}\label{eq:relative-cube-t-action}

\end{equation}
The integral identifies $H^1(Q,{\partial_x Q};\Z/2)$ with $\Z/2$. A cocycle is $dt$, with $t$ constant on each of the two faces, and the integral is the difference of those constants. Hence, $U_{\Phi_Q}$ gives a $T$ gate on the relative cube code.

title: The power of time reversal in Hamiltonian property testing
abstract: Quantum algorithms enable Heisenberg-limited scaling across many tasks in sensing and learning, achieving precision $\varepsilon$ using $O(1/\varepsilon)$ total evolution time. However, in Hamiltonian property testing, the best known algorithms have $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ total evolution time, unless it is possible to $\textit{reverse}$ the flow of time under the Hamiltonian. In this work, we prove that time reversal is necessary to close this gap. We establish evolution time lower bounds for Hamiltonian certification and locality testing, for a continuous family of error metrics ranging from average- to worst-case. We also prove matching upper bounds for Hamiltonian certification in all cases, both with and without time reversal, showing that the advantage from time reversal persists. Our results follow from a new Fourier-analytic approach to quantum lower bounds in continuous time, which is sensitive to time reversal and applicable beyond Hamiltonian property testing. This gives an alternative proof that inverses are required for amplitude amplification and estimation, improving the lower bounds of Tang and Wright and extending to fractional queries. We also show that, for unstructured search, uncertainty in the phase of the oracle destroys the quantum speedup without inverse queries, even when the oracle is fixed and coherent. Our work rigorously establishes time reversal as a resource governing both the precision of quantum measurement and the robustness of quantum algorithms.
summary:
**TL;DR** The paper proves that without the ability to run Hamiltonian evolution backwards, Hamiltonian certification and locality testing are stuck at the standard quantum limit: $\Omega(\min\{1/\varepsilon^2,\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon\})$ total evolution time, versus $O(1/\varepsilon)$ with time reversal. Matching upper and lower bounds are given for certification in all normalized Schatten $p$-norms ($p\in[2,\infty]$): $\Theta(\min\{\varepsilon^{-p}, d^{1-1/p}/\varepsilon\})$ forward-only vs. $\Theta(\min\{\varepsilon^{-p/2}, d^{1/2-1/p}/\varepsilon\})$ with reversal. The engine is a new Fourier-analytic lower-bound method (Efron–Stein plus a positive-definite kernel inequality) that is intrinsically sensitive to the sign of evolution times.

**The big picture** Many quantum tasks promise precision that improves linearly with the time you let a system evolve, but for testing properties of an unknown Hamiltonian the best known algorithms are quadratically worse — unless you can also evolve the system backwards in time. This work shows that running time backwards is genuinely necessary, not just convenient: no amount of ancillas, adaptivity, or short-time evolution can recover the better scaling with forward evolution alone. The same framework shows that inverse queries are needed for amplitude amplification and estimation, and that unknown but fixed phase errors in a search oracle destroy the quadratic speedup entirely unless inverses are available. This identifies time reversal as a quantifiable computational resource, on par with quantum memory or adaptivity in the hierarchy of learning resources.

**Key contributions**
- First forward-vs-reverse separations in the *continuous-time* model (arbitrary fractional/short-time queries), where prior separations were only for integer discrete queries.
- Tight certification complexity across the whole average-to-worst-case norm family, including the high-precision regime $\varepsilon\ll 1/\sqrt{d}$ previously uncovered.
- Improves Tang–Wright's amplitude-estimation bound from $\Omega(\min\{1/\varepsilon^2,d\})$ to $\Omega(\min\{1/\varepsilon^2,\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon\})$, and extends it to fractional queries (where the compressed-oracle argument breaks down).
- $\Omega(d\Delta)$ lower bound for Grover search with unknown coherent phase errors $\theta_x\in[\pi-\Delta,\pi+\Delta]$, contrasted with an $\tilde O(\sqrt d)$ algorithm using inverses via QSP.

**How it works** All results reduce to one "block distinguishing task": zero Hamiltonian versus $\sum_j \boldsymbol h_j\Pi_j$ with $\Pi_j$ rank-$\lfloor d/d_{\rm eff}\rfloor$ diagonal projectors and $\boldsymbol h_j=\mathrm{Ber}(\mathsf p)\cdot\mathrm{Unif}([\theta_0-\sigma,\theta_0+\sigma])$; making the blocks high-rank decouples dimension from precision. Random angles prevent the algorithm from synthesizing a self-inverse operator. The analysis proceeds one *random variable* at a time (vector-valued anchored Efron–Stein inequality) rather than one query at a time (the hybrid method only yields the useless $O(\varepsilon^2T^2)$). A coarse-grained sum-over-paths tracks whether each block was visited, reducing distinguishability to a quadratic form in the kernel $K(x,y)=\mathbb E_\omega(1-e^{ix\omega})(1-e^{-iy\omega})$. The crux: via Plancherel, $K\preceq \frac{\pi(\theta_0+\sigma)^2}{\sigma}\min(x,y)$ *only* when all $x_i\ge0$ — an explicit counterexample with $\pm t$ shows failure otherwise, pinpointing exactly where forward-only access enters.

**Why it matters** Relevant to Hamiltonian learning/testing, metrology, and query complexity: it tells experimentalists when investing in echo/time-reversal control buys a quadratic win, and gives query-complexity theorists a technique that survives fractional queries where compressed oracles fail.

**Caveats** The hard instances are non-local Hamiltonians; Heisenberg-limited forward-only certification is already known for local Hamiltonians, so locality assumptions evade these bounds. Matching upper bounds are given only for certification, not locality testing (where tightness is claimed only for $\varepsilon\gg1/\sqrt d$, constant $k$). Bounds on the actual cost of *simulating* time reversal are only implicit and likely loose. $p$ is treated as constant in asymptotics.

title: The practical cost of magic state cultivation
abstract: Magic state cultivation is a promising method for preparing high-fidelity non-Clifford resource states - a central component of fault-tolerant quantum computing - with low spacetime overhead. In benchmarking cultivation, existing resource estimates assume access to noiseless transversal measurement of the output magic state to allow for postselection during the final escape stage of the cultivation process. However, such measurements would destroy the magic state and are therefore unavailable during computation. We develop an open-boundary postselection method, Caliper, that uses only nondestructive mid-circuit syndrome information and substantially outperforms existing methods operating under these constraints. In some regimes, our postselection method uniquely recovers the resource efficiency of prior estimates. However, in other cases, we observe a tradeoff. At spacetime costs reported in previous works, the achievable logical error rates can be orders of magnitude higher, and recovering the reported logical error rate requires substantially larger codes and longer escape stages. Our results highlight how practical considerations involving mid-circuit postselection can impact the design and performance of magic state cultivation protocols.

\begin{abstract}

In benchmarking cultivation, existing resource estimates assume access to noiseless transversal measurement of the output magic state to allow for postselection during the final “escape” stage of the cultivation process. However, such measurements would destroy the magic state and are therefore unavailable during computation. We develop an open-boundary postselection method, Caliper, that uses only nondestructive mid-circuit syndrome information and substantially outperforms existing methods operating under these constraints. In some regimes, our postselection method uniquely recovers the resource efficiency of prior estimates. However, in other cases, we observe a tradeoff. At spacetime costs reported in previous works, the achievable logical error rates can be orders of magnitude higher, and recovering the reported logical error rate requires substantially larger codes and longer escape stages. Our results highlight how practical considerations involving mid-circuit postselection can impact the design and performance of magic state cultivation protocols.

Quantum error correction (QEC) is believed to be critical for reliable quantum computation at large
scales \cite{shor_scheme_1995, steane_error_1996, knill_resilient_1998,
aharonov_fault-tolerant_2008, kitaev_fault-tolerant_2003, terhal_quantum_2015, fowler_surface_2012}.
Recent experiments have demonstrated QEC on neutral-atom processors
\cite{bluvstein_logical_2024, bluvstein_fault-tolerant_2026, reichardt_fault-tolerant_2025, computing2026quantumerrorcorrectiontoric},
superconducting chips \cite{acharya_suppressing_2023, acharya_quantum_2025, krinner_realizing_2022},
and other platforms \cite{ryan-anderson_realization_2021, postler_demonstration_2022,
paetznick_demonstration_2024, abobeih_fault-tolerant_2022}.
Performing computation on encoded information, however, also requires fault-tolerant non-Clifford
operations, which are necessary for universal quantum computation \cite{gottesman_heisenberg_1998, knill_fault-tolerant_2004,
bravyi_universal_2005, eastin_restrictions_2009, zeng_transversality_2011}. 

Magic state cultivation \cite{chamberland_very_2020, itogawa_efficient_2025, gidney_magic_2024,
rosenfeld_magic_2025, sahay2026fold, vaknin_high_2026, claes_cultivating_2025, chen_efficient_2025,
hirano2026efficient} has recently emerged as a leading approach for preparing magic states with low
logical error rates, which can then be consumed to implement non-Clifford gates
\cite{gottesman_demonstrating_1999, zhou_methodology_2000, knill_fault-tolerant_2004,bravyi_universal_2005,
litinski_magic_2019}. Relatively noisy magic states begin in small codes \cite{li_magic_2015, gidney_cleaner_2023} and are continuously
refined through measurements of Clifford stabilizers and postselection \cite{chamberland_fault-tolerant_2019, chamberland_very_2020, itogawa_efficient_2025}. As the post-selected logical
error rates decrease, the code must be rapidly enlarged to protect the high-fidelity state in the
so-called ``escape'' stage. As this interface is noisy, further postselection is required,
implying repetitions that inflate the expected spacetime volume. The escape stage is the most
expensive component of cultivation \cite{sahay2026fold}, so its postselection overhead is critical
to the viability of the protocol.

Recent work has addressed this challenge by using sliding-scale postselection
\cite{bombin_fault-tolerant_2024, smith_mitigating_2024,
english_thresholds_2025, meister_efficient_2024, lee_efficient_2026, xie_simple_2026,
wills_forced_2026}, achieving a tunable balance between post-selected error rate and acceptance
fraction. One such method, the \emph{complementary gap} \cite{gidney_yoked_2023,
bombin_fault-tolerant_2024}, can achieve exponential error suppression at
high acceptance fractions \cite{bombin_fault-tolerant_2024, smith_mitigating_2024,english_thresholds_2025,
chen2026scalable}. It has therefore been employed across Refs.~\cite{gidney_magic_2024,
sahay2026fold, vaknin_high_2026, claes_cultivating_2025, hirano2026efficient} to facilitate a
low-overhead escape stage. However, its use as a diagnostic requires a closed temporal boundary from a terminal measurement at the end of a circuit to yield a useful result.
Applied directly to a mid-circuit observable, the complementary gap collapses into a narrow band whose width is independent of code distance, obscuring the differences in reliability needed for postselection
(Supplementary Material). Existing simulations close this boundary using information from a
noiseless transversal measurement of the output codeblock. In practice, this measurement would
destroy the magic state, so the decoder must instead decide whether to retain it using only
nondestructive syndrome information.

    \caption{\textbf{Magic state cultivation with mid-circuit postselection.} (a) Stages
    of the fold-transversal cultivation protocol on the surface code from Ref. \cite{sahay2026fold},
    which targets a logical error rate of $2 \times 10^{-6}$. Full error detection is used in the

This creates two challenges: without the readout, less information is available, and extracting a
reliable postselection metric from the remaining syndrome can be computationally expensive. These
considerations motivate studying escape-stage postselection under realistic, mid-circuit conditions,
where the magic state is preserved rather than measured. We refer to this setting as
\emph{open-boundary postselection}.

In this Letter, we develop an efficient method, \emph{Caliper}, for postselection
using only the syndrome information available at decision time, with latency comparable to computing
the complementary gap. We find that existing efficient heuristics
\cite{lee_efficient_2026, staples_scalable_2026, birchall_macromux_2026} can fall orders of magnitude
short of the performance accessible from the same information. This deficiency can instead be
compensated by expending additional quantum resources, revealing a tradeoff between classical
inference and quantum overhead. Caliper substantially improves this tradeoff. Nevertheless, the
consequences remain strongly protocol dependent: while some cultivation resource estimates are
nearly unchanged, others require substantially larger codes and longer escape stages to approach
their reported logical error rates. The resulting increase in spacetime cost per accepted magic
state directly raises the resources required for non-Clifford gates, and hence for fault-tolerant algorithms whose
cost is dominated by magic state preparation.

\textit{Open-boundary postselection.---} For the cultivation circuits considered here,
minimum-weight perfect matching (MWPM) approximates maximum-likelihood decoding by retaining the
most likely error configuration in each logical class rather than summing over configurations
\cite{dennis_topological_2002, higgott_pymatching_2022, higgott_sparse_2025}. For a complete syndrome $\sigma$, let $w_0$ be the minimum weight of any error configuration consistent with the observed syndrome, and let $w_1$ denote the minimum weight of any complementary error, which differs from the minimum-weight error by a nontrivial logical operator. Both can be computed via matching \cite{hutter_efficient_2014}. The
complementary gap is defined as $G=w_1-w_0$ \cite{gidney_yoked_2023, bombin_fault-tolerant_2024}, which approximates
the conditional logical error probability $P_{\mathrm L}(\sigma)\approx e^{-G}/(1+e^{-G})$. After computing the complementary gap, a decoder makes a postselection decision on whether to accept or discard the shot based on whether this gap $G$ exceeds a tunable threshold $G^*$.

At decision time, however, the decoder only has access to a visible syndrome history $\sigma_v$. The final
readout would reveal an additional, hidden (future) syndrome $\sigma_h$, giving the complete syndrome
$\sigma=\sigma_v\oplus\sigma_h$~\cite{staples_scalable_2026}, but this information is inaccessible in practice. Instead, we average over the potential hidden syndromes, weighting each by how likely it is based on $\sigma_v$: $\tilde P_L(\sigma_v)=\sum_{\hat\sigma_h}P(\hat\sigma_h\mid\sigma_v)P_{\mathrm
L}(\sigma_v\oplus\hat\sigma_h)$.

Replacing each logical class by its minimum-weight error configuration gives
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:decoding-failure-likelihood}
    \hat P_L(\sigma_v)
    = \frac{\sum_{\hat\sigma_h}e^{-w_1(\sigma_v\oplus\hat\sigma_h)}}
    {\sum_{\hat\sigma_h}\left[e^{-w_0(\sigma_v\oplus\hat\sigma_h)}
    +e^{-w_1(\sigma_v\oplus\hat\sigma_h)}\right]}.
\end{equation}
Evaluating
Eq.~\eqref{eq:decoding-failure-likelihood} requires a search over exponentially many hidden
syndromes, making it challenging to identify, at low computational cost, the
hidden syndromes that contribute most strongly to the estimated logical failure probability.

\textit{Caliper.---} Caliper is a soft-output decoder that
approximates the likelihood of an eventual logical error with low latency. Caliper approximates
Eq.~\eqref{eq:decoding-failure-likelihood} over a set $\mathcal S$ of hidden syndromes selected by
its search, and reports the open-boundary postselection score $R \approx -\log \hat P_L^{(\mathcal S)}$.
Large $R$ indicates a reliable shot, which is accepted when $R\geq R^*$. This plays the role of $G$ for open-boundary postselection, but requires searching for the hidden syndromes that dominate the estimated logical error probability and combining their contributions.

We illustrate the key idea in Fig.~\ref{fig:caliper}. Caliper begins by decoding only the visible
syndrome, with hidden detectors connected to the boundary at zero weight. The decoder finds a minimum-weight
correction whose endpoints in the hidden layer define an initial prediction $\hat\sigma_{h_0}$, with
weight $w_0^*=w_0(\hat\sigma_{h_0})$. Fixing this prediction and decoding the opposing logical
class gives $w_1(\hat\sigma_{h_0})$. These two calls to MWPM determine the complementary gap
$G_{h_0}=w_1(\hat\sigma_{h_0})-w_0^*$ if the hidden syndrome were indeed $\hat{\sigma}_{h_0}$, 
but it does not account for other possible outcomes, whose importance depends both on how likely they are and on the probability of a
logical error if they occur. Equation~\eqref{eq:decoding-failure-likelihood} combines these two
considerations: for a fixed visible syndrome, each predicted hidden syndrome contributes to the estimated logical
error probability in proportion to $e^{-w_1(\hat\sigma_h)}$.

Our key observation is that the structure of minimum-weight matching allows this space to be
explored efficiently. Moving a $-1$ syndrome from $u$ to $v$ changes the optimal correction
weight by at most the shortest-path distance between them, accounting for the logical parity of the
path. The required graph distances
can all be precomputed once for the circuit (Supplementary Material), immediately bounding the weights for nearby syndromes.

Furthermore, flipping one hidden detector requires changing the minimum-weight correction only along a path starting at that detector. Caliper can therefore search for the new correction using precomputed distances, calling MWPM only when needed to resolve the smallest weights. This enables Caliper to explore the neighborhood of a syndrome without decoding every prediction separately.

Caliper uses this observation to traverse the hidden-syndrome space in Fig.~\ref{fig:caliper}.
Starting from $\hat\sigma_{h_0}$, it evaluates hidden syndromes that differ by one hidden detector value
and preferentially continues from those with low $w_1$. This directs the search toward the syndromes
that contribute most strongly to the estimated logical error probability. Caliper also permits
steps that increase $w_1$ during an initial exploration period, subject to certain constraints.
In the Supplementary Material, we extend the search to exhaust the frontier and increase its
budget, finding only marginal reductions in logical error rate in the regimes of interest at a
substantial increase in evaluation time. 

Despite exploring a large number of hidden
syndromes, for $f=3$ surface code cultivation, Caliper spends only tens of nanoseconds on each prediction, thanks to the precomputed
graph distances. The resulting latency is within a factor of two of computing the complementary
gap in closed-boundary postselection (End Matter).

\textit{Numerical simulations.---} With Stim \cite{gidney_stim_2021}, we simulate $\ket{\bar Y}$ state cultivation---an efficient proxy
for $\ket{\bar T}$ state simulation---using the circuits of Refs.~\cite{gidney_magic_2024,
sahay2026fold, scc_fd5_simulation}, which we respectively refer to as color and (fold-transversal) surface code cultivation. We use the
same circuits and circuit-level depolarizing noise model (SD6), with physical error rate
$p=10^{-3}$, and compare the logical error rate achieved as a function of the escape-stage
postselection strength.

The results are shown in Fig.~\ref{fig:comparison}. Across all panels, Caliper achieves an equal or
lower logical error rate at any fixed discard rate than the other open-boundary methods tested. For the fault distance 3
($f=3$) color code cultivation, it performs nearly indistinguishably from the closed-boundary curve,
which most other methods also approximately follow. By contrast, in $f=3$ surface code cultivation,
the lowest achieved logical error rates are separated from closed-boundary performance by at least
an order of magnitude. Even full error detection on the visible syndromes achieves an error rate of $1.4\times10^{-5}$,
exceeding the target by almost an order of magnitude. Caliper alone smoothly
interpolates down to this performance. Our low-noise bound for full error detection (Supplementary
Material) suggests that the separation may reflect fundamental limits of the available information.

In the larger $f=5$ color code scheme, Caliper outperforms existing methods by orders of magnitude
at the relevant acceptance fractions. For instance, producing $\ket{\bar T}$ states at logical error rates of $10^{-7}$ is a common primitive in proposed fault-tolerant architectures \cite{gidney_magic_2024, zhou_resource_2025, sun2026foldedsurfacecodearchitecture, fazio2025lowoverheadmagicstatecircuits, khalid2026impactsdecoderlatencyutilityscale}.
Caliper reaches this target with an expected spacetime volume per accepted state only $10\%$
above that of closed-boundary postselection. The frozen gap \cite{birchall_macromux_2026},
the only other method we benchmarked to reach this error rate, requires approximately $7\times$
the closed-boundary volume. Reaching the more stringent $10^{-9}$ target with Caliper
requires an escape-stage acceptance fraction of $6.4\%$, compared with $23.7\%$ for
closed-boundary postselection. The expected spacetime volume is therefore approximately
$3.7\times$ larger. Even accepting only a few percent of shots, the $f=5$ surface code protocol \cite{fault_distance_4} under open-boundary postselection exhibits a logical error around $10^{-7}$.

A curious suggestion from Figure~\ref{fig:comparison} is that the performance gap between open- and closed-boundary postselection appears far larger for surface code cultivation than color code cultivation. As it turns out,
these protocols differ considerably in the size of their escape stages. For $f=3$ surface code
cultivation, the code is grown to $d=7$ and $r=3$ rounds of stabilizer measurements are performed
before deciding whether to keep the attempt. The $f=3$ color code escape stage instead uses $r=9$
rounds in a $d=15$ grafted code---roughly a $14\times$ larger syndrome. This motivates studying
modifications to the surface code escape stage.

Indeed, in Fig.~\ref{fig:modified-escape}, we independently vary the escape distance and number of QEC
cycles before running Caliper. Increasing the number of rounds alone leads to only an incremental
reduction in logical error rate, despite a $d=7$ surface code being large enough to maintain a rate
of order $10^{-6}$ per cycle. 
Recovering the target \(2\times10^{-6}\) requires increasing both the distance and the number of rounds, contrary to the usual expectation that \(d\) rounds of repeated syndrome extraction equate to a noiseless transversal measurement. Among the escape stages studied, the expected spacetime volume needed to reach this target is
minimized with $r=6$, $d=11$, and $50\%$ escape-stage acceptance. This results in an escape stage roughly
$5\times$ the size reported in Ref.~\cite{sahay2026fold}, translating to roughly a $5\times$
increase in expected spacetime volume for the entire protocol.

Finally, we study the discrepancy between open- and closed-boundary postselection, tracing it in part to rare shots in which the hidden syndrome substantially \textit{erodes} the closed-boundary gap (End Matter). These shots can be readily discarded using the readout but cannot be identified from visible information alone. We develop a phenomenological theory of this effect and hypothesize that a large escape stage is needed to keep the noisy interface between the cultivation and escape stages far from both the spatial boundaries of the code and the open temporal boundary in order to mitigate erosion.

\textit{Outlook.---} Our results show that fast and accurate mid-circuit postselection can be
implemented on matchable codes. In some instances, Caliper recovers the logical error rates
reported under closed-boundary postselection at nearly unchanged spacetime cost. However, for
other protocols and target error rates, the cost of cultivation in practice may be significantly
larger than previously expected, raising the resource overheads of architectural proposals based on
its closed-boundary performance \cite{gidney2025factor, zhou_resource_2025, cain_shors_2026, webster2026pinnacle, xue2026factoring,
khan2026architecting, yoder2025tour}. Recent work has also developed exact simulations of non-Clifford $\ket{\bar T}$ cultivation
\cite{li2025soft, chase_clifft_2026, takada2026exactefficientsimulationnoisy,
hartweg_comparing_2026, wan_exact_2026, chan_diagnosing_2026, tuloup_computing_2026}, some finding discrepancies with $\ket{\bar Y}$
proxies. An exact simulation with open-boundary postselection is therefore an important direction
for determining how realistic escape stages affect these discrepancies.

Nevertheless, it may be possible to mitigate the cost of practical postselection by optimizing escape protocols. For example, adaptive escape schemes \cite{mishima2026adaptive} could reserve large escape stages for rare, high-risk shots (Supplementary Material), reducing the average overhead required to achieve high fidelities. Simultaneously, more sophisticated inference, including ensembling \cite{shutty_efficient_2026} and machine
learning \cite{gu_scalable_2026, bonilla_ataides_neural_2026, dentelski2026neural, blue_machine_2026,
baireuther_machine-learning-assisted_2017, baireuther_neural_2019, lacroix_scaling_2025,
bausch_learning_2024, meinerz_scalable_2022, bluvstein_fault-tolerant_2026,lange_data-driven_2025,
cao_generative_2025, liu_decoding_2025, hu2025efficient, zhang2025learning}, could improve on Caliper's performance.
Neural decoders, in particular, can provide postselection metrics based on decoder confidence that
approximate a logical gap and outperform the surface code complementary gap in closed-boundary
experiments \cite{gu_scalable_2026, dentelski2026neural, bausch_learning_2024}. Extending these metrics to open boundaries
poses challenges analogous to those for the complementary gap, and adapting them will require training
to estimate the probability of eventual decoding failure using only the visible syndrome. Caliper
can provide a benchmark for this task.

We expect the broader lessons on realistic postselection to extend to resource-state
preparation with high-rate quantum low-density parity-check codes \cite{menon_magic_2025, jacob_single-shot_2025, li_transversal_2025, hetenyi2026constantdepthmagicstate}. The analogue of an
escape stage for these protocols should likewise be co-designed with mid-circuit postselection.

\textit{Algorithmic description of Caliper.---} Algorithm~\ref{alg:caliper} summarizes the search.
The distance table stores minimum path weights between graph nodes, including the spatial boundaries of the code. Caliper sums over all evaluated predictions in $\mathcal S$ to estimate $R$. For weights not known exactly, it uses the smallest correction weight found so far.

\begin{algorithm}[H]
    \caption{Caliper}\label{alg:caliper}
    \footnotesize
    \begin{algorithmic}[1]
        \Require Visible syndrome $\sigma_v$, distance table, limits $b,B$, depth and branching limits
        \State Decode $\sigma_v$ with hidden detectors free to obtain $\hat\sigma_{h_0}$ and $w_0(\hat\sigma_{h_0})$.
        \State Fix $\hat\sigma_{h_0}$ and decode the opposing logical class to obtain $w_1(\hat\sigma_{h_0})$.
        \State Initialize $\mathcal S \gets \{\hat\sigma_{h_0}\}$, $\mathcal Q \gets \{\hat\sigma_{h_0}\}$; $n\gets 0$.
        \While{$\mathcal Q\ne\varnothing$ and $n<B$}
            \State Take $\hat\sigma_h$ with lowest estimated $w_1$ from $\mathcal Q$.
            \State $\mathcal N \gets$ hidden syndromes differing from $\hat\sigma_h$ by one hidden detector value.
            \State Bound the matching weights using the distance table, then tighten the bounds by updating known corrections.
            \State Use MWPM as needed to determine the smallest weights.
            \State Store the weight estimates and bounds; $\mathcal S\gets\mathcal S\cup\mathcal N$.
            \State $n\gets n+1$.
            \State Select predictions in $\mathcal N$ whose bounds allow $w_1$ to stay the same or decrease, favoring low estimates of $w_1$ and respecting the depth and branching limits.
            \If{$n\leq b$ and $\mathcal N\ne\varnothing$}
                \State Also select the prediction in $\mathcal N$ with lowest estimated $w_1$.
            \EndIf
            \State Add selected predictions to $\mathcal Q$ only if not previously queued.
        \EndWhile
        \State \Return $R$ from Eq.~\eqref{seq:implemented-score}.
    \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}

\textit{Latency.---} A critical aspect of any mid-circuit postselection metric is the speed at which
it can be computed. Its result directly determines the subsequent computation, so the quantum
computation must idle in the meantime \cite{fowler_time-optimal_2012, gidney_flexible_2019}. By using precomputed graph distances, Caliper achieves a
latency comparable to computing the complementary gap. Caliper is written primarily in \verb|C++|; for $f=3$ surface code cultivation, Caliper takes a median of $25.3\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ per shot, compared with
$15.5\,\mu\mathrm{s}$ for the closed-boundary complementary gap (measured over $10^4$ shots) on one core of
an Apple M4 processor. 

It can be further accelerated since, in practice, Caliper needs only to determine whether the score exceeds the acceptance threshold $R^*$.
Shots with an initial score sufficiently far below $R^*$ can often be discarded before exploring
further hidden syndromes. We set this early-rejection criterion from the observed changes in $R$ during
the search. Figure~\ref{fig:latency-ridgeline} compares the resulting decision latencies with those
of the thresholded closed-boundary gap.
