On neutral-atom hardware, where a standard QEC cycle has a timescale on the order of milliseconds \cite{bluvstein_fault-tolerant_2026, computing2026quantumerrorcorrectiontoric}, Caliper applied to the $f=3$ protocols is fast enough to output a decision without additional idling. The larger protocols may require faster execution or a modest number of additional QEC cycles to bridge the reaction time \cite{gidney_flexible_2019, gidney_magic_2024}. On the microsecond timescales of superconducting hardware \cite{acharya_quantum_2025}, however, both the complementary gap—even with a closed boundary—and Caliper may require substantial acceleration, potentially using specialized hardware such as FPGAs \cite{das_scalable_2022, holmes_nisq_2020, liyanage_scalable_2023, wu_micro_2025}. In part, this is because, from our estimates, identifying the most likely class takes tens of microseconds, while the MWPM calculation for the complementary class can be up to $30\times$ slower. Without such acceleration, the spacetime cost of preserving the state while awaiting the postselection decision could dominate the cost of cultivation.

\textit{Calibration.---} An ideal postselection method is well-calibrated, which means that it can
accurately predict the posterior LER that will occur at whatever postselection strength we choose.
Calibration is not strictly necessary for a postselection method to perform well; clustering-based
metrics \cite{lee_efficient_2026}, for example, do not predict the post-selected LER but can still rank shots by how likely to
fail they seem. Nevertheless, calibration provides an illuminating diagnostic: it allows us to test
whether a method’s estimated confidence faithfully reflects the observed distribution and, when it
does not, to empirically investigate why.

In Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}, we plot a reliability diagram for Caliper, along with closed-boundary
complementary gap. A perfectly calibrated metric would follow the $y=x$ line, where the predicted
and actual probabilities of logical failure are identical. Even in the closed-boundary setting, the
complementary gap appears miscalibrated, consistently underestimating logical error rates. The
reason for this overconfidence is well-understood: the predicted logical error rate is computed from
the complementary gap $G$ as $\hat P_L \approx e^{-G}/(1+e^{-G})$ \cite{gidney_yoked_2023, bombin_fault-tolerant_2024}, but it neglects the entropic factors
that describe the number of degenerate error mechanisms that produce gap $G$, along with higher-gap
mechanisms \cite{dennis_topological_2002, duclos-cianci_fast_2010}. At low but finite $p$, the contribution from higher-gap
mechanisms is negligible, leaving only the number of degenerate gap $G$ mechanisms, $N(G)$. The
closed-boundary calibration curve is well-described by a linear relationship on the log-log plot of
Fig.~\ref{fig:calibration}; a linear fit achieves $R^2 \simeq 0.97$ and slope $1-T$, where $T \simeq 0.18$
describes the effective (dimensionless) temperature of the system. For reference, the perfect calibration line corresponds to zero effective temperature, which is realized in the $p \rightarrow 0$ limit \cite{nishimori_internal_1981, dennis_topological_2002}.  

From the fit, we also obtain an empirical entropy model with prefactor $c_0$:
\begin{equation}
    \hat N(G) \approx c_0 e^{-(1-T)G}/e^{-G} = c_0 e^{TG}.
\end{equation}
This is consistent with our expectation that with a gap of $G$, the domain wall excitation
corresponds to a string of length $L\propto G$, and there are $N_L\propto \exp(L)$ such strings, so
the entropy of the system scales as $\Delta S \propto \log N(G) \propto G$ \cite{dennis_topological_2002}. Precisely in this sense,
as $T \rightarrow 0$, the closed-boundary curve is perfectly calibrated since the complementary
gap's zero-temperature approximation becomes exact.

For the open-boundary setting, Caliper consistently underestimates the logical error rate by an even
wider margin than the complementary gap. Moreover, its calibration curve is manifestly non-linear.
In part, this is because the failure probability conditioned on the open-boundary score $R$ depends
indirectly on $R$. By the tower property,
\begin{align}
    \Pr(\text{Fail} \mid R) & = \E_{G \sim \rho_{G \mid R}} [\Pr(\text{Fail} \mid G, R) \mid R]
\end{align}
This is averaged over, and thus depends on, the distribution of gaps $G$ given $R$, $\rho_{G \mid
R}$. To leading order, the conditional LER depends only on $G$: $\Pr(\text{Fail} \mid G, R) \approx
\Pr(\text{Fail} \mid G)$, where the only $R$-dependence in the conditional LER is through $\rho_{G
\mid R}$, and we numerically verify this behavior (SM). The non-linearity of the calibration curve
is also expected to arise from $\rho_{G \mid R}$.

Thus, we study $\rho_{G \mid R}$ in further empirical detail and summarize here the results; a more
thorough discussion can be found in the Supplementary Material. We observe that for the most part,
the closed-boundary complementary gap $G$ and Caliper score $R$ are close. However, in a select few instances, the
hidden syndrome reveals information that results in $G \ll R$: a phenomenon we call
\textit{erosion}. $\Delta = R - G$ measures the shortfall of the realized gap relative to the open-boundary
score, with larger $\Delta$ leading to larger discrepancies between the LER predicted
by Caliper and reality. It is even possible for a maximally large open-boundary score $R$ to erode to
a near-zero gap, at which point the decoding result is effectively random. That said, erosion is
rare. Outside of $R \sim G$, we find that the probability $R - G = \Delta$ is exponentially
suppressed in $\Delta$, where $\rho(G \mid R) \approx A e^{-\kappa \Delta}$. The eroded fraction of
shots at $R$ is
\begin{equation}
    E_R = \int_{0}^{R} \rho d\Delta = E_\infty (1 - e^{-\kappa R}),
    \label{eq:erosion-fraction}
\end{equation}
where $E_\infty=A/\kappa$ is the asymptotic eroded fraction in this model.
A shot at $R$ either did not erode and fails at a closed-boundary gap $R$ or erodes by $\Delta$ and
fails at a gap $R - \Delta$. Noting that $\rho(\Delta) \rightarrow 0$ exponentially quickly as
$\Delta \rightarrow \infty$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:phenomenological-description}
    \Pr(\text{Fail} \mid R) \approx [1 - E_R] c_0 e^{-(1-T)R} + B e^{-\kappa R},
\end{equation}
where $T$ is the same temperature as in the closed-boundary setting and $B$ is the amplitude of
the contribution from eroded shots. We determine $\kappa$ from
the negative slope of a weighted linear fit to $\log\rho(\Delta)$ versus $\Delta$, excluding the
peak near $\Delta=0$. For each $\Delta$, we pool shots with $R\geq\Delta$; the fitted amplitude
gives $A$.

\section{Guarantees from Caliper}
\label{sec:caliper}

In this section, we establish the properties of matching that allow Caliper to efficiently search
over possible hidden syndromes. Throughout, we work in the most-likely-error approximation used in
the main text. Exact maximum-likelihood decoding is $\#\mathrm{P}$-hard in general
\cite{iyer_hardness_2015}. As an efficient proxy, matching retains only the most likely error
configuration in each logical class.

\subsection{Matchable detector error models}

\begin{definition}[Detector error model]
    Consider a circuit subject to a set $\mathcal E$ of independent elementary error mechanisms.
    Each mechanism $\varepsilon\in\mathcal E$ occurs with probability $p_\varepsilon$ and flips a
    set of detectors $\partial\varepsilon$. It may also flip the logical observable, in which case
    we call $\varepsilon$ \emph{marked}. The collection of error mechanisms together with their
    detector syndromes, logical outcomes, and probabilities defines the detector error model (DEM)
    of the circuit.
\end{definition}

For an error configuration $E\subseteq\mathcal E$, the observed syndrome is
\begin{equation}
    \partial E
    =
    \bigoplus_{\varepsilon\in E}\partial\varepsilon ,
\end{equation}
and its logical outcome is the parity of the marked mechanisms in $E$. Since the mechanisms occur
independently,
\begin{equation}
    P(E)
    =
    \prod_{\varepsilon\in E}p_\varepsilon
    \prod_{\varepsilon\notin E}(1-p_\varepsilon)
    =
    \kappa e^{-w(E)},
\end{equation}
where $\kappa$ is independent of $E$ and
\begin{equation}
    w(E)
    =
    \sum_{\varepsilon\in E}\omega_\varepsilon,
    \qquad
    \omega_\varepsilon
    =
    \log\!\left(\frac{1-p_\varepsilon}{p_\varepsilon}\right).
    \label{seq:dem-weight}
\end{equation}
As in the main text, weights and scores use natural logarithms. Where figures quote values in dB,
the conversion is $10/\ln 10$ dB per natural-log unit. We assume the weights are positive.

\begin{definition}[Matchable DEM]
    A detector error model is \emph{matchable} if every elementary error mechanism flips at most two
    detectors,
    \begin{equation}
        |\partial\varepsilon|\leq 2
        \qquad
        \text{for all }\varepsilon\in\mathcal E .
    \end{equation}
\end{definition}

A matchable DEM has a weighted graph representation. Each detector is represented by a vertex. A
mechanism that flips two detectors $u$ and $v$ gives an edge between $u$ and $v$, while a mechanism
that flips a single detector is connected to a virtual boundary vertex. Boundary vertices carry no
detector constraint. Each edge has weight $\omega_\varepsilon$, and an edge is marked exactly when
the corresponding mechanism flips the logical observable. Parallel edges may be retained.

For a detector syndrome $S$, a \emph{correction} is an edge set $M$ whose odd-degree detector
vertices are precisely $S$; no parity constraint is imposed on virtual boundary vertices. Its weight
is
\begin{equation}
    \|M\|
    =
    \sum_{\varepsilon\in M}\omega_\varepsilon .
\end{equation}
Let $W_0(S)$ and $W_1(S)$ be the minimum weights of corrections with even and odd marked-edge
parity, respectively. We write
\begin{equation}
    w_0(S)=\min\{W_0(S),W_1(S)\},
    \qquad
    w_1(S)=\max\{W_0(S),W_1(S)\}.
\end{equation}
The complementary gap is therefore
\begin{equation}
    G(S)=w_1(S)-w_0(S).
\end{equation}

Because all edge weights are positive, a minimum-weight correction contains no unnecessary closed
loops. It may therefore be written as a collection of paths pairing syndrome defects either with one
another or with a boundary. Replacing every such path by a shortest path cannot increase the weight.
This gives the usual reduction to minimum-weight perfect matching.

It will be useful below to keep track of the logical parity of a path. Let
\begin{equation}
    d_b(u,v),\qquad b\in\{0,1\},
\end{equation}
denote the minimum weight of a path from $u$ to $v$ containing marked edges of parity $b$. These
distances depend only on the DEM and can therefore be precomputed. They can be obtained by running
shortest-path search on the graph in which each vertex is doubled according to the accumulated
marked-edge parity. When the logical parity is irrelevant, we write
\begin{equation}
    d(u,v)=\min\{d_0(u,v),d_1(u,v)\}.
\end{equation}

For a decoding graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges, the full distance table can be constructed by repeated Dijkstra searches in $O(V(V + E) \log V)$ time and stored in $O(V^2)$ memory. Tracking logical parity changes these costs only by constant factors. The table is computed once for each circuit and noise model and is reused across shots. 

\subsection{Changing a syndrome}

We now establish the basic observation used by Caliper. Suppose a syndrome $S$ is changed to
$S\oplus T$, where $T$ is a set of detector flips. Let $M$ be a minimum-weight correction for $S$.
For any edge set $J$, define its net cost relative to $M$ by
\begin{equation}
    c_M(J)
    =
    \sum_{\varepsilon\in J\setminus M}\omega_\varepsilon
    -
    \sum_{\varepsilon\in J\cap M}\omega_\varepsilon .
    \label{seq:net-cost}
\end{equation}
This is exactly the change in weight produced by replacing $M$ by $M\oplus J$.

\begin{lemma}[Exact change under a syndrome modification]
    \label{slem:increment}
    Let $M_\ell$ be a minimum-weight correction of syndrome $S$ in logical class $\ell$. Then
    \begin{equation}
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus T)-W_\ell(S)
        =
        \min_J c_{M_\ell}(J),
        \label{seq:increment}
    \end{equation}
    where the minimum is over edge sets $J$ whose odd-degree detector vertices are exactly $T$ and
    whose marked-edge parity is $b$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
    For every allowed $J$, the edge set $M_\ell\oplus J$ has syndrome $S\oplus T$ and logical class
    $\ell\oplus b$. Hence
    \begin{equation}
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus T)
        \leq
        W_\ell(S)+c_{M_\ell}(J).
    \end{equation}
    Minimizing over $J$ gives one inequality.

    Conversely, let $M'$ be a minimum-weight correction of $S\oplus T$ in class $\ell\oplus b$. Then
    \begin{equation}
        J=M_\ell\oplus M'
    \end{equation}
    has detector boundary $T$, marked-edge parity $b$, and
    \begin{equation}
        c_{M_\ell}(J)
        =
        \|M'\|-\|M_\ell\|
        =
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus T)-W_\ell(S).
    \end{equation}
    Thus the bound is attained.
\end{proof}

The important special case is the relocation of a syndrome defect from $u$ to $v$, for which
$T=\{u,v\}$.

\begin{corollary}[Distance bound]
    \label{slem:distance-bound}
    For any $u,v$ and $b\in\{0,1\}$,
    \begin{equation}
        \left|
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus\{u,v\})
        -
        W_\ell(S)
        \right|
        \leq
        d_b(u,v).
        \label{seq:distance-bound}
    \end{equation}
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
    Let $J$ be a minimum-weight $u$--$v$ path of marked-edge parity $b$. Toggling $J$ transforms any
    correction for $(S,\ell)$ into a correction for $(S\oplus\{u,v\},\ell\oplus b)$ and changes its
    weight by at most $\|J\|=d_b(u,v)$. Hence
    \begin{equation}
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus\{u,v\})
        -
        W_\ell(S)
        \leq d_b(u,v).
    \end{equation}
    Applying the same path in the reverse direction gives the opposite inequality.
\end{proof}

Thus the effect of relocating a defect can always be bounded using a table lookup. The exact change
depends on how the path intersects the current correction, through Eq.~\eqref{seq:net-cost}, but its
magnitude is bounded independently of the shot.

Caliper frequently does better than this bound by explicitly considering the possible local
modifications of the current correction.

\begin{lemma}[Certificate for an exact local update]
    \label{slem:cert}
    Let $\mathcal J_{\rm loc}$ be a set of candidate modifications with the required syndrome and
    logical parity, and define
    \begin{equation}
        c_{\rm loc}
        =
        \min_{J\in\mathcal J_{\rm loc}} c_M(J).
    \end{equation}
    Suppose $\lambda$ is a lower bound on $c_M(J)$ for every allowed modification $J\notin\mathcal
    J_{\rm loc}$. If
    \begin{equation}
        c_{\rm loc}\leq\lambda,
    \end{equation}
    then
    \begin{equation}
        W_{\ell\oplus b}(S\oplus T)-W_\ell(S)
        =
        c_{\rm loc}.
    \end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
    By Lemma~\ref{slem:increment}, the exact change is the minimum net cost over all allowed
    modifications. Every modification outside $\mathcal J_{\rm loc}$ has cost at least $\lambda$,
    while a modification inside $\mathcal J_{\rm loc}$ has cost $c_{\rm loc}\leq\lambda$. Hence the
    global minimum lies in $\mathcal J_{\rm loc}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Update after flipping one detector]
    \label{slem:chain}
    For the decoding graphs used here, let $M$ be a minimum-weight correction in one logical
    class, written as paths pairing defects or connecting them to a boundary. After flipping
    a hidden detector $u$, a minimum-weight
    correction in the same class can be found by reconnecting these pairs along one path
    starting at $u$ and ending at a boundary. The change in weight is the total weight of the
    new connections minus that of the removed ones.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
    Compare the pairs in $M$ with those in a minimum-weight correction after the flip. The
    connections appearing in only one correction form a path from $u$ to a boundary, together
    with closed loops and paths between boundaries. Each remaining loop or boundary-to-boundary
    path preserves all detector values and the logical class. Its net cost must be zero: a negative
    cost would improve $M$, while a positive cost would improve the new correction when
    reversed. We can therefore omit these loops and paths, leaving only the path starting at $u$.
\end{proof}

Caliper explores these reconnections using the precomputed distances. It reuses calculations
for the same partial update and stops exploring a choice once its lower bound exceeds the best
update found so far. Once every possible update has been checked or ruled out by the bounds,
the matching weight is exact. The calculation is repeated for both logical classes, then the
two weights are ordered as $w_0\leq w_1$.

If this calculation is too large or reaches its search limit, Caliper continues with bounds
on the weights. It improves these bounds where possible and uses MWPM as needed to identify
the smallest weights. A further decode may also be needed to construct the correction used
in the next search step. Some weights can remain approximate.

\textit{Simulation settings.---} In the main text, we use $b=6$ and $B=18$, select up to ten
neighbors by the non-increasing rule, and apply this rule only when expanding a prediction
within three flips of the initial prediction. The exact update calculation uses limits of
63 defects, 57 matched pairs, and successive limits of $2048$, $32768$, and $524288$ partial
updates. The margins for additional decoding and for correction updates are $2.5$ and $5$,
respectively, in natural-log units.

There is a particularly useful case in which no change to the gap is possible.

\begin{lemma}[Cancellation away from the critical path]
    \label{slem:cancel}
    Let $M_0$ and $M_1$ be minimum-weight corrections for syndrome $S$ in the two logical classes.
    Suppose a class-preserving modification $J$ is certified by Lemma~\ref{slem:cert} to be optimal
    for both class corrections. If
    \begin{equation}
        J\cap(M_0\oplus M_1)=\varnothing,
        \label{seq:no-critical-intersection}
    \end{equation}
    then
    \begin{equation}
        G(S\oplus T)=G(S).
    \end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
    Equation~\eqref{seq:no-critical-intersection} implies that every edge of $J$ either belongs to
    both $M_0$ and $M_1$ or to neither. Therefore
    \begin{equation}
        c_{M_0}(J)=c_{M_1}(J).
    \end{equation}
    Since $J$ preserves the logical class and is optimal for both modified matching problems,
    Lemma~\ref{slem:increment} shows that $W_0$ and $W_1$ change by exactly the same amount. Their
    difference is therefore unchanged.
\end{proof}

The symmetric difference $M_0\oplus M_1$ is the part of the matching that distinguishes the two
logical classes. Lemma~\ref{slem:cancel} therefore formalizes the intuition used by Caliper:
hidden-syndrome modifications that do not interact with this region can often be shown to leave the
complementary gap exactly unchanged.

\begin{abstract}
We give a shadow tomography algorithm that uses $O(\log(m) \log(m/\delta) / \varepsilon^2)$ copies of the input state. 
Specifically, given a quantum state $\rho$ and observables $O_1,\ldots,O_m$, the algorithm outputs estimates of $\tr(O_i\rho)$ for all $i\in[m]$ that are all accurate to within $\pm\varepsilon$, except with probability at most $\delta$.

The key idea is to work in the average-case setting: for a random state drawn from a known prior, a pretty good measurement on $O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$ copies gives a constant-error guarantee on all but a small fraction of the prior. 
Boosting this guarantee gives an average-case shadow tomography algorithm, and the minimax principle then (non-constructively) implies the existence of a measurement with the same worst-case guarantee. 

We also identify an obstruction to further improvement with this approach.
While pretty good measurements amplify success over the randomness of the prior, they do not amplify success over the randomness of measurement.

This issue appears to be inherent, and gives rise to the remaining $\log(m)$ factor separating the complexity of the quantum problem from its classical counterpart.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Measuring quantum states is delicate business.

Observing a state necessarily disturbs it, so if we measure where it lies along one axis, we destroy the information of where it lies along a different axis.
This central property of quantum mechanics is known as \emph{measurement uncertainty}, and like Heisenberg uncertainty, it arises because observables need not commute with each other.
Unlike in the classical world, where observables commute happily, it matters in which order we apply measurements to quantum states, as states degrade with each successive measurement; we grapple with this issue every time we try to extract information from quantum states.

Measurement uncertainty has been formalized many times across almost a century of literature.
Early literature focuses on quantifying the tradeoff between how much information one gains from a measurement and how much disturbance it causes, starting with Heisenberg~\cite{Hei27}\footnote{Heisenberg originally described his principle in terms of how a measurement in one basis disturbs the state in another; what we know now as the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is a later refinement, capturing the slightly different phenomenon that quantum states cannot be ``certain'' (low standard deviation) with respect to two different axes, and was shown by Kennard~\cite{Ken27}, Robertson~\cite{Rob29}, and Schr\"odinger~\cite{Sch30}.} and progressively sharpened over time~\cite{AK65,AG88,FP96,Oza03,BLW13,BHOW14}; see also the review~\cite{BLW14} and the closely-related gentle measurement lemma~\cite{Win99,ON02}.

More recently, researchers have investigated more operational variants of this question, giving bounds on the quality of (unbiased) estimators for the expectations of two non-commuting observables from measuring one state~\cite{Nag89,Hay99}; see~\cite{CSLA21} for a recent exposition. 

However, essentially all of this literature focuses on the single-copy setting.

Since measurement uncertainty is a fundamental limit on single-copy measurement, we might expect the same phenomenon, and its operational consequences, to persist in the many-copy setting. 

The natural question to pose here is: does estimating non-commuting observables require more copies than estimating commuting ones?
Put another way, what is the cost of non-commutativity of measurement?
One might even expect the effect to be more than constant, an asymptotically worse statistical rate resulting from the inability to reuse states after measurement.
Little is known about this question.
Later, we discuss formulations of this question with a more statistical flavor; but in the quantum computing literature, this question is captured by the problem of \emph{shadow tomography}, posed by Aaronson in 2016~\cite{Aar16}. 

In the problem of shadow tomography, we are given copies of an unknown state $\rho$, along with some observables $O_1, \dots, O_m$.
Our goal is to estimate every expectation $\tr(O_i \rho)$ to within $\pm\eps$ accuracy with a total failure probability of at most $\delta$.
When $\rho$ is a classical distribution, there is no issue: we can reuse the same samples to estimate every observable, requiring only $O(\log(m / \delta)/\eps^2)$ samples; the $\log(m)$ comes from a union bound.

For a general quantum state, however, you run into immediate issues with non-commutativity: measuring one observable can disturb the state, preventing the measurement of the rest of them.
A naive algorithm, therefore, uses $O(m\log(m/\delta)/\eps^2)$ copies, while running full tomography requires $O(d^2/\eps^2)$ copies.
Aaronson showed that, surprisingly, shadow tomography can be solved using a number of copies that scales polynomially in $1/\eps$, $\log(m)$, and $\log(d)$~\cite{Aar18}!

Since then, subsequent work has steadily brought the sample complexity down~\cite{AR19,BO24}, until the latest work of~\cite{COPW26}, which uses only $O(\log(m)\sqrt{\log(d)}/\eps^3)$ copies.

This complexity is essentially optimal for the general approach taken by all prior work: designing sufficiently gentle measurements that reveal useful information while disturbing the state as little as possible, so that it can be reused in later rounds.

The persistent dependence on dimension suggested that this dependence might be necessary for shadow tomography, and perhaps reflects a fundamental cost of non-commutativity.

However, as we do not have any lower bound for shadow tomography stronger than $\Omega(\log(m/\delta)/\eps^2)$, the question remains open.

\subsection{Results}

We make further progress on shadow tomography with a new dimension-independent algorithm.

\begin{restatable}{theorem}{WorstCaseShadow}
\label{thm:intro-worst}
There is an algorithm for the shadow tomography problem that consumes 
\[
O\!\left(\frac{\log(m)\log(m/\delta)}{\eps^2}\right)
\]
copies of the input state.
\end{restatable}

Notably, this algorithm has no dependence on the dimension of the input state.
It gives the first dimension-free shadow tomography algorithm with only polylogarithmic dependence on $m$; prior to this work, the best dimension-free bound was $O(\sqrt{m}/\eps^2)$ copies, due to~\cite{COPW26}, improving an earlier $O(\sqrt{m}\log(m)/\eps^2)$ bound of Sinha~\cite{Sin25}.
With this, the best-known bounds for shadow tomography, with constant $\delta$, can be summarized as follows:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item $O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$ copies suffice in the high-precision regime $\eps \lesssim 1/d$~\cite{PSW25,PSTW25}. 
    

    \item $O(\log(m)\sqrt{\log(d)}/\eps^3)$ copies suffice~\cite{COPW26}; for $\eps \gtrsim 1/d$, this gives the best known bound when $\sqrt{\log(d)}/\eps \lesssim \log(m)$. 
    
    \item $O(\log^2(m)/\eps^2)$ copies suffice by this work; for $\eps \gtrsim 1/d$, this gives the best known bound when $\sqrt{\log(d)}/\eps \gtrsim \log(m)$. 
\end{enumerate}

Our key idea is to depart from previous work and study shadow tomography in the \emph{average case}, where the input state is drawn from a known prior.
Let us first state this average-case variant more formally. 
Suppose that the unknown state is promised to belong to some known family of states $\calF = \{\rho_1, \dots, \rho_\ell\}$, and let $p = (p_1, \dots, p_\ell)$ be a known prior on this family.
The input state $\brho = \rho_{\bx}$ is obtained by drawing $\bx \sim p$, and we are given copies of $\brho$ together with observables $O_1, \dots, O_m$.

As before, our goal is to output estimates of the expectation values $\tr(O_i \brho)$ for every $i \in [m]$ to accuracy $\pm \eps$. 
The key difference is that we no longer require the algorithm to succeed for every possible input state in $\calF$. 
Instead, we require the algorithm to succeed with probability at least $1-\delta$ over both the random choice of $\brho$ from the prior and the randomness of the measurement. 

Working in the average case gives us access to tools that are naturally defined with respect to a prior.
Most importantly, we can use (variants of) the \emph{pretty good measurement} (PGM), a canonical measurement first designed for the task of quantum state discrimination. 
With this, we can attain a shadow tomography algorithm in the average-case setting.

\begin{theorem}
\label{thm:intro-avg}
There is an algorithm for the average-case shadow tomography problem that consumes 
\[
O\!\left(\frac{\log(m)\log(m/\delta)}{\eps^2}\right)
\]
copies of the input state.
\end{theorem}

\Cref{thm:intro-worst} follows directly from \cref{thm:intro-avg} by Sion's minimax theorem~\cite{Sio58} (which generalizes the classical minimax theorem of von Neumann~\cite{vN28}).
We note that this approach is fundamentally non-constructive: the minimax theorem merely tells us that an algorithm exists, without giving an explicit description of one.\footnote{
The minimax measurement can in principle be found constructively by solving a semidefinite program over POVMs. 
This does not give an especially illuminating algorithm, however.
    
    
}

Indeed, this non-constructiveness may be the fundamental strength of this approach. 
As we will discuss later, a major obstacle to designing shadow tomography algorithms is that we do not understand what a hard instance looks like for any given set of observables.
The average-case formulation lets us avoid this problem entirely: rather than identifying the hardest prior, we prove that our algorithm works for \emph{every} prior, allowing the measurement to depend on the prior it is given.
The minimax theorem then turns these average-case guarantees into a worst-case guarantee without ever requiring us to identify which prior is hardest.

However, this approach appears to be bottlenecked at $\log^2(m)$.
In the next section, we will discuss why, and in the process detail our current understanding of pretty good measurements and average-case shadow tomography.

\paragraph{Concurrent work.}
Concurrent to our work, Jeronimo, Huang, and Liu attained the same complexity bound, going through similar techniques, though with a more intricate algorithm and analysis.
Though our proof is AI-generated, we can be fairly confident that it was generated independently: we first produced a shadow tomography algorithm using $O(\log^2(m)\log(m/\delta)/\eps^2)$ copies on July 28th and the algorithm presented here on August 2nd.
Jeronimo, Huang, and Liu posted their paper to arXiv on August 6th, initially attaining a $\widetilde{O}(\log^4(m/\delta)/\eps^2)$ shadow tomography algorithm, and subsequently improved the algorithm to the $O(\log(m)\log(m/\delta)/\eps^2)$ algorithm, posted on September 14th.

\paragraph{Related work on the cost of noncommutativity.}

Another natural way to investigate the cost of non-commutativity is with a statistical lens: given observables $O_1, \dots, O_m$ and $n$ copies of the state $\rho$, compute unbiased estimators $\bo_1,\dots,\bo_m$ of $\tr(O_1 \rho), \dots, \tr(O_m \rho)$ such that the total variance $\sum_i \Var[\bo_1] + \dots + \Var[\bo_m]$ is as small as possible.
In particular, the question is about the rate: as $n \to \infty$, the total variance will scale as some $C/n + o(1/n)$; the goal is to identify $C$, the dominant contribution to the rate.
For this question, results indicate that the cost of non-commutativity is at most a factor of $2$: while this variance can be as large as $m$ for commuting observables, it is at most $2m$ for non-commuting observables.
This factor of two was first described by Nagaoka and Hayashi in the single-copy setting~\cite{Nag89,Hay99} and later extended to various multi-copy settings~\cite{TAD20,CSDV19,ABR26}.
In particular, this gap is the same factor of two which separates the Quantum Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound~\cite{Hel67} from the Holevo--Cram\'{e}r--Rao bound~\cite{Hol11}, and is a direct consequence of the \emph{measurement incompatibility} that arises from non-commutativity.
This factor of two is tight; see, for example, \cite[Section 3.1.1]{DGG20}.

For these formulations, the central focus is on the variance, for which the pretty-good measurement has especially nice behavior (see \Cref{subsec:pgm-mse}).
By comparison, shadow tomography demands control of higher moments, since the desired $\log(m)$ scaling comes from demonstrating an exponential tail on the estimator distribution.
This makes the two formulations substantially different: even though the cost of non-commutativity is a constant factor for variances, it need not be the same for shadow tomography.\footnote{
Here, we have restricted our discussion to allowing for general measurements.
In restricted settings, such as requiring measurements to only operate on single copies, the cost of non-commutativity is essentially $m$: it is near-optimal to measure each observable on $O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$ copies of $\rho$, without any reuse~\cite{CCHL22}.
}

\section{Background}
\label{background}

In this section, we will describe the broad approach that we took when designing our shadow tomography algorithm, and what motivated us to consider this approach.
We will then survey several proof directions that we attempted, some of which were successful, some of which were not, and we will conclude by describing the high level proof strategy that we have ultimately decided to take.

\subsection{The pretty good measurement in full state tomography}

To motivate the approach we take to the shadow tomography problem, let us first consider the more challenging task of full state tomography.
Suppose one is given $n$ copies of an unknown state, where the state is promised to be an element of some family $\calF = \{\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_{\ell}\}$ of states.
For ease of exposition, we will assume that this family is of finite size, but in practice the state families considered in full state tomography (e.g.\ the set of all pure states) are usually infinite and continuous.\footnote{We note, however, that it always suffices to consider finite-size families, as continuous families of states can always be discretized.}
If $\rho_i$ is the unknown state, a tomography algorithm is allowed to perform any measurement on the input $\rho_i^{\otimes n}$, and its goal is to output an estimator $\widehat{\brho}$ which is close to $\rho_i$ in trace distance (with, say, 99\% probability).

There is a common two-step strategy for designing full state tomography algorithms, often achieving optimal sample complexities.
\begin{enumerate}
\item First, identify a natural ``hard'' distribution $p = (p_1, \ldots, p_{\ell})$ over the states of this family.
Ideally, solving tomography over a state drawn from this distribution should be every bit as hard as solving tomography over a worst-case state drawn from the family $\calF$.
\item Second, define the tomography algorithm to be the \emph{Pretty Good Measurement (PGM)} over this distribution of states. This is the measurement $M = \{M_1, \ldots, M_{\ell}\}$ defined as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pgm-def}
    M_i = S^{-1/2} \cdot p_i \rho_i^{\otimes n} \cdot S^{-1/2}, \text{ for all $i \in [\ell]$,}
    \qquad \text{where } S = p_1 \rho_1^{\otimes n} + \cdots + p_{\ell} \rho_{\ell}^{\otimes n}.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}
In other words, given the input $\rho_i^{\otimes n}$, the algorithm will perform the measurement $M$, receive some outcome $\bj \in [\ell]$, and output the estimator $\widehat{\brho} = \rho_{\bj}$, which is hopefully close to $\rho_i$ in trace distance.

The PGM originates from the literature on the related problem of \emph{quantum state discrimination}.
An instance of the average-case variant of quantum state discrimination is specified by a set $\calL$ of labels $x$, a set of states $\{\sigma_x\}_{x \in \calL}$ labeled by $\calL$, and a distribution $q = (q_x)_{x \in \calL}$ on the states.
It is convenient to take the set of labels to be $\calL = \{1, \ldots, \ell\}$,
but later we will sometimes view the labels as specifying a real-valued parameter of the states that we would like to compute.
Given a state $\sigma_{\bx}$ drawn from this distribution, the goal is to output $\widehat{\bx} \in \calL$ such that $\widehat{\bx} = \bx$.
Hence, viewing $\bx$ as a parameter of the state $\sigma_{\bx}$, quantum state discrimination is the difficult task of \emph{exactly} computing this parameter (whereas in full state tomography, we are only asked to approximate a given parameter).
The algorithm's success probability is given by its average case success probability over the different input states, i.e.\
\begin{equation*}
    \E_{\bx \sim q}\big[\Pr[\widehat{\bx} = \bx \mid \sigma_{\bx}]\big].
\end{equation*}
If $P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q)$ is the success probability of the optimal strategy and $\overline{P}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q) = 1 - P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q)$ is its failure probability (and similarly for $P_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q)$ and $\overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q)$),
then Barnum and Knill~\cite{BK02} showed that $P_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q) \geq P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q)^2$,
which in turn implies that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pretty-good}
    \overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q) \leq 2 \cdot \overline{P}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q).
\end{equation}
This gives a formal sense in which the PGM is ``pretty good'' and justifies the PGM's role as the canonical default measurement in quantum state discrimination.

There is no analogous justification for why the PGM should serve the same role in full state tomography, yet in practice many algorithms are designed with the above two-step strategy.

Examples include Hayashi's algorithm for pure state tomography~\cite{Hay98}, in which the chosen distribution is the Haar measure over pure states;
the tomography algorithm of~\cite{SSW25} for rank-$r$ projector states (i.e.\ states of the form $\rho = P/r$, where $P$ is a rank-$r$ projector),  in which the chosen distribution is the Haar measure over projector states;
the algorithm of~\cite{PSTW25} for general mixed state tomography based on the random purification channel, in which the chosen distribution is the Hilbert-Schmidt measure over mixed states;
and one of the two mixed state tomography algorithms of~\cite{HHJ+16}.
In all these cases, the families of states being learned are highly symmetric, allowing one to choose distributions on these states which are themselves highly symmetric. This leads to tomography algorithms which are elegant to describe and clean to analyze.

As an aside, let us note one more property of the PGM in quantum state discrimination.
If the states $\sigma_x$ \emph{are} actually tensor product states, i.e.\ $\sigma_x = \tau_x^{\otimes n}$, for some set of states $\{\tau_x\}_{x \in \calL}$, then~\cite{HW12} observed that the PGM's failure probability can always be bounded by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:pgm-fail}
    \overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q) \leq |\calL| \cdot F^n,
\end{equation}
where $F$ is the maximum pairwise fidelity between two distinct states $\tau_x \neq \tau_y$.
Crucially, this means that in the setting of quantum state discrimination, the PGM's failure probability \emph{decays exponentially} in the number of copies of the state one is given so long as this maximum fidelity is bounded away from 1, say $F \leq 1 - \epsilon$, a property we will revisit throughout this section.

\subsection{Hard distributions in shadow tomography}
\label{subsec:background-minimax}

Now let us attempt to design a shadow tomography algorithm using this strategy.
Let $O_1, \ldots, O_m$ be the observables we would like to estimate,
and let $\calF = \{\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_k\}$ be the finite family of quantum states that our unknown state is promised to be drawn from.
The first step in this strategy is to identify a natural ``hard'' distribution $p = (p_1, \ldots, p_k)$ over the states in $\calF$ for which the task of shadow tomography is every bit as hard as it is for a worst case state drawn from $\calF$.

What should this hard distribution look like?
It is perhaps difficult to answer this in a precise, formal sense, but we can list a couple of properties that it should intuitively satisfy.
First, if $\brho$ is a state drawn from this  distribution, then for every observable $O_i$, the observable value $\tr(O_i \cdot \brho)$ should have a reasonably large variance over the randomness in the state $\brho$.
If not, then one could predict $\tr(O_i \cdot \brho)$  by ignoring the input and outputting a fixed value independent of the state.
Second, for any $i \neq j$, we should want different observable values $\tr(O_i \cdot \brho)$ and $\tr(O_j \cdot \brho)$ to vary around their means in uncorrelated ways.
If instead observable values are correlated, then correctly predicting one observable would allow one to correctly predict another one, without having to take the second observable into account when designing one's measurement.

Designing distributions which satisfy these properties seems challenging, and to date, there is no canonical method to specify a hard distribution for a given set of observables.
Because of how multiple observables interact, hard distributions can be highly nonsymmetric and challenging to describe elegantly.
Surprisingly, this is still true when the observables themselves are highly structured, like the Pauli matrices $\{I, X, Y, Z\}^{\otimes k}$.

\paragraph{Worst-case quantum state discrimination.}
A similar issue has been faced before, in the literature on the \emph{worst}-case variant of quantum state discrimination.
An instance of this problem is specified only by a set of states $\{\sigma_x\}_{x \in \calL}$ (without an additional probability distribution).
Given a state $\sigma_{x}$ in this set, the goal is to output an $\widehat{\bx} \in \calL$ such that $\widehat{\bx} = x$.
The algorithm's success probability is given by its worst-case success probability over the different input states, i.e.\
\begin{equation*}
    \min_{x \in \calL}\big\{\Pr[\widehat{\bx} = x \mid \sigma_x]\big\}.
\end{equation*}
A natural way to design an algorithm for this problem is to identify a ``hard'' distribution $q = (q_1, \ldots, q_k)$ on these states and consider the PGM on this distribution. 
Exactly this approach was taken by Montanaro in the work~\cite{Mon19}, where he considered the performance of the PGM for worst-case state discrimination when defined on the uniform distribution $q = (\frac{1}{|\calL|}, \ldots, \frac{1}{|\calL|})$.
This is clearly not the \emph{hardest} distribution for most sets of states, but Montanaro's results showed that it was still ``hard enough'' to rederive some known bounds on worst-case state discrimination.
However, if one wants to build an algorithm based on the truly hardest choice of distribution $q$, then again one seems stuck, as we do not know a clean way to express exactly what this distribution is.

However, Harrow and Winter~\cite{HW12} observed a simple way to get around this issue.
They point out that a direct application of the minimax theorem shows that if $P_{\mathrm{OPT}}$ is the optimal probability of success in the worst-case setting, then
\begin{equation*}
P_{\mathrm{OPT}} = \min_q\big\{P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q)\big\}.
\end{equation*}
Hence, to lower bound the optimal success probability in the worst case,
it suffices to lower bound the optimal success probability in the average case, for all prior distributions $q$.
This eliminates the need to identify a candidate hard distribution: instead, one is directly given a distribution $q$ and can design an algorithm specifically for this distribution $q$.
Using this, Harrow and Winter were able to take average-case lower bounds on the PGM shown by Barnum and Knill~\cite{BK02} and port them over to the worst-case setting.

\paragraph{Minimax for shadow tomography.}
Inspired by this, let us consider an average-case variant of shadow tomography in which the input state $\brho$, rather than being a worst-case element of the family $\calF$, is sampled from a known prior $p = (p_1, \ldots, p_{\ell})$ on the states in $\calF$.
Let us write $\bo = (\bo_1, \ldots, \bo_m)$ for its $m$ observable values, where $\bo_i = \tr(O_i \cdot \brho)$.
A shadow tomography algorithm can be specified by a POVM $M = \{M_{\widehat{o}}\}_{\widehat{o}}$, where the measurement outcomes $\widehat{o} = (\widehat{o}_1, \ldots, \widehat{o}_m) \in \R^m$ are the predictions for the $m$ observable values.
Its success probability can be written as
\begin{equation*}
    P_{\mathrm{succ}}(p, M) \coloneqq \Pr_{\brho, \widehat{\bo}}\big[\text{for all }i \in [m], \,|\widehat{\bo}_i - \bo_i| \leq \eps\big],
\end{equation*}
where $\widehat{\bo}$ is the result of measuring $\brho^{\otimes n}$ with $M$.
The set of all probability distributions $p$ is convex, as is the set of all POVMs $M$, and $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{succ}}(p, M)$ is linear in both $p$ and $M$.
As a result, the minimax theorem tells us that
\begin{equation*}
    \max_M \min_p \{P_{\mathrm{succ}}(p, M)\} = \min_p \max_M \{P_{\mathrm{succ}}(p, M)\}.
\end{equation*}
The left-hand side is minimized at a distribution $p$ which places all its probability mass on a single, worst case input state $\rho_i$.
Hence, this tells us that
\begin{equation*}
    \max_M \min_{i \in [\ell]} \{P_{\mathrm{succ}}(\rho_i, M)\} = \min_p \max_M \{P_{\mathrm{succ}}(p, M)\}.
\end{equation*}
The left-hand side is just the probability of success of the optimal measurement for shadow tomography in the traditional, worst-case setting, and the right-hand side is just the optimal probability of success in the average-case setting with prior $p$, minimized over all prior $p$.
Hence, just as in quantum state discrimination, if we can solve shadow tomography in the average-case setting, we can solve it in the worst-case setting.

\subsection{The PGM in shadow tomography}

The basic algorithm we will consider in this work is the natural plug-in estimator associated with the pretty good measurement.
Given $\brho^{\otimes n}$, where $\brho$ is drawn from the prior $p$, it acts as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item Measure with the PGM associated with the prior $p$ on the states $\rho_1^{\otimes n}, \ldots, \rho_{\ell}^{\otimes n}$. Let $\bi \in [\ell]$ be the measurement outcome, and set $\widehat{\brho} = \rho_{\bi}$.
    \item Output $\widehat{\bo}_1 = \tr(O_1 \cdot \widehat{\brho})$, \ldots, $\widehat{\bo}_m = \tr(O_m \cdot \widehat{\brho})$.
\end{enumerate}
Surprisingly, this natural strategy has not previously been considered in the literature.
All previous attempts which have achieved sample complexity which is polylogarithmic in $m$ (as well as in $d$) have operated in the general framework proposed by Aaronson in his very first shadow tomography paper in~\cite{Aar18}, in which one maintains a hypothesis state $\widehat{\brho}$ which serves as one's guess for the true state, and one repeatedly updates $\widehat{\brho}$ by finding observables whose values it predicts incorrectly.
Most of the algorithms considered in these works apply to the online setting, in which one has to predict the value of the first observable before being given the second, and so on, and it is known that any algorithm in the online setting whose sample complexity is polylogarithmic in $m$ must also have at least a $\sqrt{\log(d)}$ dependence on the dimension.

A subset of our authors were originally convinced that the PGM strategy above \emph{must} be the right strategy for achieving sample complexity $O(\log(m))$, as it is mathematically elegant, and Math is typically fair.
Furthermore, presuming that it \emph{does} work, there is a clear path towards proving it,
which we formalize in the following conjecture.

\begin{conjecture}[PGM Decay Conjecture]
For any observable $O \in \C^{d \times d}$ with $\Vert O \Vert_{\infty} \leq 1$,
    \begin{equation*}
        \Pr\big[|\tr(O \cdot \widehat{\brho}) - \tr(O \cdot \brho)| > \eps\big] \leq O\big(C^{-n \epsilon^2}\big),
    \end{equation*}
    for some absolute constant $C >0$.
    Here, $\brho$ and $\widehat{\brho}$ are distributed as above.
\end{conjecture}

\noindent
If this conjecture were true, then applying it to the observables $O_1, \ldots, O_m$, we would have that, by a union bound,
\begin{equation*}
    \Pr\big[\text{exists $k \in [m]$ such that }|\widehat{\bo}_k - \bo_k| > \eps\big] \leq O(m \cdot C^{-n \epsilon^2}),
\end{equation*}
where we recall that $\bo_k = \tr(O_k \cdot \brho)$, for each $k \in [m]$ (and similarly for $\widehat{\bo}_k$).
Then if we set $n = O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$, the PGM will succeed with probability at least .99, as desired.
Note that as we have observed in \Cref{eq:pgm-fail} above, the PGM's failure probability \emph{does} decay exponentially as a function of the number of copies $n$ in the setting of quantum state discrimination, and so it is reasonable to hope that a similar behavior should occur here as well.
Unfortunately, the PGM Decay Conjecture actually turns out to be \emph{false}, and there are examples of families $\calF$, priors $p$, and observables $O$ in which the error probability of the PGM decays as $1/\poly(n)$ rather than our desired $1/\exp(n)$. In the next few subsections, we will discuss natural attempts at proving the PGM Decay Conjecture and why these fail, as these failures will illuminate features that our eventual algorithm will have.

Let us note one interesting feature of the above algorithm: the measurement does not depend on the observables we are trying to estimate;
these are only taken into account when the measurement outcome is classically post-processed.
In the traditional, worst-case setting, an algorithm for performing shadow tomography whose measurement does not depend on the observables is said to be solving the \emph{classical shadows} problem (named after the algorithm in the work~\cite{HKP20}), and it is known that classical shadows algorithms cannot succeed with $n = O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$ copies. Indeed, the work of Grier, Pashayan, and Schaffer~\cite{GPS24} shows that classical shadows algorithms require $\widetilde{\Omega}(\sqrt{d})$ copies, even to estimate a single observable.
However, these bounds only apply to the worst-case setting, and it is consistent with our state of knowledge that a $O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$-copy classical shadows algorithm could exist in the average case setting (indeed, we conjecture that this is the case).
As we have shown, this would imply an $O(\log(m)/\eps^2)$-copy algorithm for shadow tomography in the worst case. How could this be, given that we have worst-case lower bounds against classical shadows algorithms?
The answer is that the worst-case algorithm this reduction would produce is equal to the average-case algorithm for the prior $p$ which is hardest for the observables $O_1, \ldots, O_m$, and this prior would presumably encode the observables $O_1, \ldots, O_m$.

\subsection{A mean-squared error bound for the PGM} \label{subsec:pgm-mse}

The first difficulty one encounters when trying to prove the PGM Decay Conjecture is that very little work has been done on the PGM, outside of the literature on quantum state discrimination.
Results from this literature will help us understand with what probability the PGM will \emph{perfectly} identify the input state (or, perhaps, some feature of the input state),
but in our setting we only want the PGM to \emph{approximately} identify the input state, in a very weak sense (i.e.\ it should find a state which is close to the input on the observable $O$).
As a result, existing tools do not seem to apply to our setting.
The one exception we are aware of is the work of Mishra, Lami, and Wilde~\cite{MLW26},
who proved bounds on the ability of the PGM to approximately predict some feature of the input state.

\subsubsection{The Mishra--Lami--Wilde bound}
\label{sec:mishra-lami-wilde}

To state their result, suppose we have a set of states $\{\sigma_x\}_{x \in \calL}$, where the label set $\calL$ is a subset of $[-1, 1]$, and let $q = (q_x)_{x \in \calL}$ be a prior on this set.
We think of the label $x \in \calL$ as encoding some parameter of the state $\sigma_x$ that we would like to predict;
given a state $\sigma_{\bx}$ drawn from the prior $p$, the goal of an algorithm is to output a value $\widehat{\bx} \in \R$ such that $\widehat{\bx}$ is close to $\bx$.
(This is in contrast with the traditional setting of quantum state discrimination, where we only care about identifying $\bx$ exactly.)
The \emph{mean-squared error (MSE)} of the algorithm is given by
\begin{equation*}
    \E_{\bx \sim p} \big[\E_{\widehat{\bx}} (\widehat{\bx} - \bx)^2\big].
\end{equation*}
Let us write $\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{OPT}}$ for the minimal MSE achievable by an algorithm on the prior $p$, and let us write $\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{PGM}}$ for the MSE that the PGM achieves.
Then the main result of~\cite{MLW26} is that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mlw}
\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{PGM}} \leq 2 \cdot \mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{OPT}}.
\end{equation}
This is the analogue of the Barnum and Knill~\cite{BK02} bound from \Cref{eq:pretty-good} in the setting of estimating a parameter of a state, and the proofs of these two statements are similar.

Let us now apply this bound to derive a consequence related to the PGM Decay Conjecture.
Let $O \in \C^{d \times d}$ be an observable with $\Vert O \Vert_{\infty} \leq 1$ that we wish to estimate, and let $\calF = \{\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_{\ell}\}$ be our family of states.
For simplicity, we will assume that the observable values $\tr(O \cdot \rho_1), \ldots,\tr(O \cdot \rho_{\ell})$ are distinct,
and we will define the label set to be $\calL = \{\tr(O \cdot \rho_i)\}_{i \in [\ell]}$.
In addition, we will set the states and prior as follows: for the observable value $o \in \calL$ corresponding to the state $\rho_i \in \calF$, we set $\sigma_o = \rho_i^{\otimes n}$ and $q_o = p_i$.
Now we can apply the main result of \cite{MLW26}, which says that \Cref{eq:mlw} holds in this setting.

To interpret what this means, let us first understand what the PGM looks like for this ensemble.
First, the average of the states is
\begin{equation*}
    S
    = \sum_{o \in \calL} q_{o} \cdot \sigma_{o}
    = \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} p_i \cdot \rho_i^{\otimes n}.
\end{equation*}
In addition, for each $o \in \calL$, the POVM element associated with the label $o$ is given by
\begin{equation*}
    M_{o} = S^{-1/2} q_{o} \sigma_{o} S^{-1/2}
    = S^{-1/2} p_i \rho_i^{\otimes n} S^{-1/2},
\end{equation*}
where $\rho_i$  is the state in $\calF$ with observable value $o$.
This is identical to the PGM that we get from the ensemble $\{\rho_i^{\otimes n}\}$ with prior $p$, except with the output label classically post-processed via the mapping $i \mapsto o_i$.
The fact that the PGM is well-behaved under classical post-processing was previously observed and applied in the prior work of~\cite{KT08,BJL23,LdW25} and the independent and concurrent work of~\cite{AG26}, who referred to it as the PGM being ``closed under coarse-graining''.

Next, let us understand the optimal strategy (in terms of the mean-squared error) for estimating the observable  $O$.
One strategy for doing this, though perhaps not precisely \emph{the} optimal one, is to simply measure the observable $O$ on each copy of the input state independently and then average the results. 
To analyze this, let us first condition on the input state $\rho \in \calF$, and write $o$ for its observable value.
Write $\widehat{\bx}^1, \ldots, \widehat{\bx}^n$ for the results of the $n$ measurements, and let $\widehat{\bx}$ be their average.
Then each $\widehat{\bx}^i$ is an unbiased estimator for the true observable value, meaning $\E[\widehat{\bx}^i] = o$, and each $\widehat{\bx}^i$ falls within the interval $[-1, 1]$ (since $\Vert O \Vert_{\mathrm{op}} \leq 1$).
This means that $\Var[\widehat{\bx}^i]\leq 1$ for all $i$, and so $\Var[\widehat{\bx}] \leq 1/n$, since $\widehat{\bx}$ is their average.
As a result, we can bound the MSE of this algorithm by
\begin{equation*}
    \E_{\brho \sim p} \big[\E_{\widehat{\bx}} (\widehat{\bx} - \bo)^2\big]
    =  \E_{\brho \sim p} \big[\Var[\widehat{\bx} \mid \brho]\big]
    \leq \E_{\brho \sim p}[1/n] = 1/n.
\end{equation*}
This then implies that $\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{OPT}} \leq 1/n$ as well, since this is the MSE of the algorithm with minimal MSE.
Hence, by \Cref{eq:mlw}, we have
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mse-for-one-observable}
\E_{\brho \sim p} \big[\E_{\widehat{\bo}} (\widehat{\bo} - \bo)^2\big]
=
\mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{PGM}} \leq 2 \cdot \mathrm{MSE}_{\mathrm{OPT}} \leq 2/n.
\end{equation}
Then a simple application of Markov's inequality tells us that $|\widehat{\bo} - \bo| \leq \epsilon$
except with probability $2/(n \epsilon^2)$.
This is similar to our desired bound in the PGM Decay Conjecture, though much weaker than it: we are hoping for a bound which is inverse exponential in $n \epsilon^2$, whereas this is only inverse polynomial.

For later, let us briefly note that the strategy from above satisfies a stronger form of concentration than just a mean-squared error bound.
In particular, since $\widehat{\bx}$ is an average of $n$ independent random variables contained in $[-1, 1]$, a Hoeffding bound will tell us that $|\widehat{\bx} - \bo| \leq \epsilon$ except with probability $2 e^{-n\epsilon^2/2}$.

\subsubsection{A new shadow tomography guarantee}

Even though this bound doesn't achieve the PGM Decay Conjecture, it still allows us to say something new and interesting about shadow tomography. 
Let $O_1, \ldots, O_m$ be the $m$ observables we would like to estimate,
and let $\widehat{\bo}_1, \ldots, \widehat{\bo}_m$ be the predictions made by the PGM-based shadow tomography algorithm.
Then applying \Cref{eq:mse-for-one-observable} to each observable separately, we have that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mse-by-linearity}
    \E_{\brho\sim p} \E_{\widehat{\bo}} \Vert \widehat{\bo} - \bo \Vert_2^2
    = \E_{\brho \sim p} \E_{\widehat{\bo}}\sum_{i=1}^m (\widehat{\bo}_i - \bo_i)^2
    = \sum_{i=1}^m \E_{\brho \sim p}  \E_{\widehat{\bo}}(\widehat{\bo}_i - \bo_i)^2
    \leq \sum_{i=1}^m 2/n = 2m/n.
\end{equation}
We will try to interpret what this bound means shortly.
First, though, let us observe that although this is an average-case guarantee, one can use a similar minimax argument as before to show that it implies a worst-case guarantee as well.
In particular, doing so implies the following statement.

\begin{proposition}[Mean-squared error bound for shadow tomography]\label{prop:mse}
    For any observables $O_1, \ldots, O_m \in \C^{d \times d}$ with $\Vert O_i \Vert \leq 1$,
    there exists an algorithm such that given $n$ copies of an unknown (worst-case) state $\rho \in \C^{d \times d}$, the algorithm outputs estimates $\widehat{\bo}_1, \ldots, \widehat{\bo}_m \in [-1, 1]$ such that
    \begin{equation*}
        \E_{\widehat{\bo}} \Vert \widehat{\bo} - o \Vert_2^2 \leq \frac{2m}{n},
    \end{equation*}
    where $o_i = \tr(O_i \cdot \rho)$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$.
\end{proposition}

To understand this bound, note that Markov's inequality implies that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:just-markoved}
    \Vert \widehat{\bo} - o \Vert_2^2 \leq O(m/n)
\end{equation}
with probability at least .99. If, for example, we set $n = O(1/\eps^2)$ to be large enough, then when this occurs, we have
\begin{equation*}
    \Vert \widehat{\bo} - o \Vert_2^2 \leq \frac{1}{100} m \eps^2.
\end{equation*}
An averaging argument then implies that for at least 99\% of the observables, we have $|\widehat{\bo}_i - o_i| \leq \epsilon$, whereas at most $1\%$ of them violate this.
More generally, given $O(\frac{1}{\alpha\eps^2})$ copies of $\rho$, we have an algorithm which, with probability $\geq 0.9$ (amplifiable through the median trick), accurately estimates a $1-\alpha$ fraction of the observables to within $\eps$ error.
This already is a non-trivial result: Aaronson considers this setting in \cite{Aar07}, and proposes a PAC learning approach to solving it.
His algorithm uses $\widetilde{O}(\frac{\log(d)}{\eps^2 \alpha})$ copies; we recover this complexity without the dimension dependence.
We note that a similar guarantee, with a similar high level proof strategy, had previously appeared in the literature on quantum random access codes (QRACs) due to a result of~\cite{LdW25}, which gives an algorithm for extracting most, but not all, of the bits of a QRAC.

Unfortunately, though, we do not necessarily know \emph{which} of the observables are incorrect; if we did, we could simply recurse on these ``bad'' observables in order to achieve a $\poly(\log(m),1/\epsilon)$ sample complexity.
Without knowing which are bad, then, the only obvious way to use this guarantee to estimate all $m$ observables is to apply \Cref{eq:just-markoved} with $n = O(m/\epsilon^2)$ copies, giving us
\begin{equation*}
    \Vert \widehat{\bo} - o \Vert_2^2 \leq \epsilon^2.
\end{equation*}
For this to be true, it must be that $|\widehat{\bo}_i - o_i| \leq \epsilon$ for all $1 \leq i \leq m$.
However, even trivial algorithms for shadow tomography can achieve $n = O(m/\epsilon^2)$ copies, making this sample complexity not so interesting.

All that said, the bound in \Cref{prop:mse} is still quite interesting, because we do not know any way to achieve this sort of mean-squared error guarantee without going through the PGM and the minimax theorem.
Early in the project, we viewed this as an encouraging sign that the PGM was the ``right'' approach to shadow tomography.
Not only that, the bound in \Cref{prop:mse} is the optimal bound that one can show on the mean-squared error of a shadow tomography algorithm.
To see this, we first note that this statement for general $m$ reduces to the case when $m = 1$.
This is because if we have an example of a prior and an observable $O$ such that any algorithm must satisfy $\E(\widehat{\bo}- \bo)^2 \geq \Omega(1/n)$, then we could simply take our $m$ observables to be $O_1 = \cdots = O_m = O$,
and then any algorithm must satisfy $\E \Vert \widehat{\bo} - \bo \Vert_2^2 \geq \Omega(m/n)$ by linearity.
Then, in the $m = 1$ case, an example of a prior and observable for which any algorithm must satisfy $\E(\widehat{\bo} - \bo)^2 \geq \Omega(1/n)$ is given by
\begin{align*}
    p_1 = p_2 = \frac{1}{2},\quad
    \rho_1 &= \Big(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big) \cdot\ketbra{0} + \Big(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big) \cdot\ketbra{1},\\
    \rho_2 &= \Big(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big) \cdot\ketbra{0} + \Big(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\Big) \cdot\ketbra{1}, \quad
    O = \ketbra{0}.
\end{align*}
Although we will not prove that the bound holds in this case, intuitively it is because $n$ samples are needed to estimate the bias of a coin up to error $1/\sqrt{n}$.

\subsection{Negative results for the PGM}

Following our success with the mean-squared error bound, we made various attempt at deriving $\poly\log(m)$-copy shadow tomography algorithms using the PGM, either by establishing the PGM Decay Conjecture or by other means.
In this subsection, we give an overview of some of these attempts, explain why they fail, and describe what they say about what an eventual PGM-based shadow tomography algorithm must look like.

\subsubsection{Bootstrapping the mean-squared error bound?}\label{sec:bootstrap}

Given nonnegative weights $w_1, \ldots, w_m$, consider the weighted mean-squared error given by
\begin{equation*}
    \E_{\brho \sim p} \sum_{i=1}^m w_i \cdot (\widehat{\bo}_i - \bo_i)^2.
\end{equation*}
If $w_1 + \cdots + w_m = m$, then the same argument that established \Cref{eq:mse-by-linearity} also implies that the weighted MSE of the PGM is at most $2m/n$.
Based on this, one strategy we tried was to ``bootstrap'' the seemingly-weak weighted mean-squared error bounds into an algorithm with $\polylog(m)$ copy complexity by repeatedly performing the PGM and adjusting the weights we use when calculating its weighted mean-squared error.
For example, suppose we run the PGM on our state with $n = O(1/\epsilon^2)$ copies.
As we have seen, it will correctly estimate 99\% of the observables up to error $\epsilon$, with reasonably high probability.
Now, suppose there \emph{was} a way, using our knowledge of the prior distribution $p$ and the values that the PGM output, to infer which of these predictions we have higher confidence in, and which of these predictions we have lower confidence in.
Then we could perform the PGM again, and this time when we analyze its mean-squared error, we could place more weight on those observables whose predictions we are less confident about, forcing the output of the second PGM to be more accurate on these observables than the first PGM was.
We could then repeat this until we are confident about all the observables.

\paragraph{A Pauli counterexample.}
Unfortunately, there is a simple counterexample which shows that this approach, at least as stated here, cannot work.
In this counterexample, let us suppose that $d$ is a power of $2$, and let our observables $O_1, \ldots, O_m$ be $m$ pairwise anticommuting Pauli matrices.
Let the family of states be $\calF=\{\rho_1, \ldots, \rho_m\}$, where for each $1 \leq i \leq m$,
\begin{equation*}
\rho_i = \frac{I + O_i}{d},
\end{equation*}
and let the prior be $p = (\tfrac1m,\ldots,\tfrac1m)$.
Then
\begin{equation*}
    \tr(O_j \cdot \rho_i) =
    \left\{\begin{array}{rl}
            1 & \text{if $i = j$,}\\
            0 & \text{otherwise}
            \end{array}\right.
\end{equation*}
Thus, performing shadow tomography on these $m$ observables with the error parameter set to a small constant, say $\eps = 0.1$, is equivalent to identifying which state one is given.
Now, suppose that after the first step of our bootstrapping scheme, the PGM returns $\widehat{\bo}_1, \ldots, \widehat{\bo}_m$ satisfying
\begin{equation}\label{eq:step-one-of-the-bootstrap}
    \Vert \widehat{\bo} - \bo \Vert_2^2 \leq O(m/n) = O(m\epsilon^2) = (\text{a very small constant}) \cdot m.
\end{equation}
To achieve this bound, it could be that the PGM simply outputs $\widehat{\bo}_1 = \cdots = \widehat{\bo}_m = 0$, which would satisfy the even stronger bound
\begin{equation*}
    \Vert \widehat{\bo} - \bo \Vert_2^2 = 1.
\end{equation*}
This is a possible output if the only property we use of the first PGM is that its outputs satisfy \Cref{eq:step-one-of-the-bootstrap}. But this tells us nothing interesting, as we could have output these values even without looking at the input state, and so we cannot use this to bootstrap any further.

Incidentally, another reason that bootstrapping fails on this example, at least for the particular form of bootstrapping that we consider here, is that if one only performs PGM measurements, then solving this example requires performing entangled measurements across $n = \Omega(\log(m))$ copies at a time (so, $O(1/\eps^2)$ copies at a time does not suffice).
This is because it can be shown that when the PGM is performed on this example with $t = o(\log(m))$ copies, the result will essentially be a uniformly random label in $[m]$, except with a slight bias towards the true label $i$,
in which case the PGM would have to be repeated many times before one could extract the true label.

\subsubsection{A high probability version of the Barnum--Knill bound?}
\label{sec:general-quantum-case}

In the previous section, we saw that the PGM inherits the mean-squared error guarantee of the optimal algorithm, with a factor-2 loss.
What if the optimal algorithm exhibits stronger forms of concentration? Will the PGM inherit these too?

In the setting of \Cref{sec:mishra-lami-wilde}, in which we have a prior $(q_x)_{x \in \calL}$ on states $\{\sigma_x\}_{x \in \calL}$, let us consider the probability that the algorithm succeeds at estimating the parameter $\bx$ of the input state $\sigma_{\bx}$, meaning that its output satisfies $|\widehat{\bx} - \bx| \leq \epsilon$.
Let us write $P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q, \epsilon)$ for the success probability of the optimal measurement (and $\overline{P}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q, \epsilon) = 1 - P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q, \epsilon)$ for its failure probability), and define $P_{\mathrm{PGM}}$ and $\overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}}$ similarly. Could it be that, say
\begin{equation}\label{eq:conjectured-bk-analogue}
    P_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q, \epsilon) \geq P_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q, \epsilon)^2,
    \quad \text{and therefore} \quad
    \overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}}(q,\epsilon) \leq 2 \cdot \overline{P}_{\mathrm{OPT}}(q, \epsilon)?
\end{equation}
This would be a natural analogue of the Barnum--Knill bound in \Cref{eq:pretty-good}, except to the problem of approximately computing a parameter, rather than exactly computing it.
And a bound of this form would be enough to prove our PGM Decay Conjecture.
This is because as noted in \Cref{sec:mishra-lami-wilde} above, there is an algorithm whose probability of failure can be bounded by $2e^{-n\epsilon^2/2}$, and so the probability of failure of the optimal algorithm can as well. 
Therefore, \Cref{eq:conjectured-bk-analogue} would imply that $\overline{P}_{\mathrm{PGM}} \leq 4 e^{-n\epsilon^2/2}$, as claimed by the PGM Decay Conjecture.

\end{align*}

\begin{equation*}

\end{equation*}

The vectors $\ket{\psi_i}$ with $i$ small are ``local'' in the sense that they put very similar coefficients on standard basis vectors $\ket{j}$ which have similar values of $j$, whereas when $i$ is large, these vectors are ``nonlocal'', and may put very different coefficients on two nearby basis vectors.
The vectors $\ket{v_i}$ are similarly ``local'', and put most of their amplitude on the Fourier vectors $\ket{\psi_i}$ with small $i$,
and the matrix $S$ also has most of its eigenweight placed on these ``small $i$'' Fourier vectors.
Inverting this, $S^{-1/2}$ will therefore place a \emph{large} amount of weight on these ``large $i$'' Fourier vectors, and so multiplying by it will serve to amplify the weight on the ``large $i$'' Fourier vectors. This means that the $\ket{w_i} = S^{-1/2} \cdot \ket{v_i}$ vectors will have their mass much more spread out than the $\ket{v_i}$ vectors in the standard basis, and so measuring a vector $\ket{v_i}$ with the PGM will often result in a faraway measurement outcome $M_j$.

\subsubsection{Making use of the tensor product structure?}
\label{sec:tensor}

The counterexample in the previous section shows that we probably cannot hope to prove the PGM Decay Conjecture by proving a statement about the PGM's success probability on a generic, unstructured ensemble of states, and then use it to derive the PGM Decay Conjecture as a special case (in the same way that we could derive \Cref{eq:mse-for-one-observable} as a special case of \Cref{eq:mlw}).
Instead, we would have to use specific properties about our particular ensemble, namely the fact that our ensemble consists of $n$-fold tensor products of $d$-dimensional states (whereas the counterexample in \Cref{sec:general-quantum-case} is not a tensor product). Could this be the missing piece?

\paragraph{A single qubit counterexample.}
We were able to generate numerical evidence suggesting that the answer was still no, and that in fact the PGM sometimes has subexponential decay, perhaps as bad as $e^{-\sqrt{n}}$.
This evidence was based on an ensemble of $\ell$ qubit pure states $\ket{v_0}, \ldots, \ket{v_{\ell}}$ of the form
\begin{equation*}
\ket{v_i}=
\cos(\theta_i) \cdot \ket{0} + \sin(\theta_i) \cdot \ket{1},
\end{equation*}
with the $\ell$ angles, very roughly, being evenly spaced between $0$ and $\pi/2$ (so that $\theta_i \approx i \cdot \pi/(2(\ell-1))$).
We considered various ways to modify the PGM to thwart this ensemble, without success.
These included adding noise to the ensemble, with the hope of combating the issue of $S$ being poorly conditioned, as well as considering other variants of the PGM. To expand on this, the PGM is defined by computing the $S$ matrix, and then setting the measurement operator $M_i$ equal to $q_x \sigma_x$ ``divided by'' $S$.
There is, however, no unique way to define what it means to divide one matrix $A$ by another matrix $B$.
The traditional definition of the PGM takes this to mean $B^{-1/2} A B^{-1/2}$, but there is another natural way to divide matrices based on the Sylvester superoperator,
and yet another based on the derivative of the matrix logarithm. This last one corresponds to what is known as the ``integral PGM'', which was first considered in the work~\cite{CL26a} and has more recently been applied in~\cite{CL26b}.
